title: Autocatalytic Closure: An AGI Research Program Based on Non-equilibrium Thermodynamics
abstract: Autocatalytic Closure: An AGI Research Program Based on Non-equilibrium Thermodynamics Wang Fengqing(School of Automation Engineering, Northeast Electric Power University, Jilin 132012, China) Abstract: [Objective] This paper addresses four puzzles in artificial intelligence, the diminishing returns of scaling, persistent hallucination, catastrophic forgetting, and inexhaustible tail risk, which have so far been discussed separately without a unified explanation. [Methods] Adopting non-equilibrium thermodynamics as a programmatic language, it proposes the establishment of an autocatalytic closure as the physical criterion for AGI, together with a trinity of high-entropy exploration, low-entropy selection and organogenesis, operationalized by a three-gate mechanism; a two-stage correction experiment (N=2) serves as a proof-of-concept. [Results] The four puzzles are uniformly attributed to the heterocatalytic open-loop nature of current systems; drawing on the Anthropic 2026 report and self-verification precedents, the paper diagnoses that frontier practice still operates in the open-loop stage. [Limitations] The N=2 experiment is only a mechanistic illustration, and the engineering feasibility of the three-gate mechanism remains unverified. [Conclusions] The criterion of AGI should be the establishment of an autocatalytic closure, and falsifiable schemes are provided. Keywords: autocatalytic closure; dissipative structure; low-entropy selection; organogenesis emergence; AGI criterion

title: Quantum Topology and Machine Learning Synergy: A Collaborative Optimization Framework
abstract: Quantum topology, a fascinating field of physics, offers unique properties that could revolutionize machine learning. This paper investigates the potential of combining quantum topology with machine learning to achieve enhanced data analysis and predictive modeling. We propose a novel framework that leverages the inherent characteristics of quantum topology to create a synergistic approach, enabling more robust and accurate results. The core mechanism involves incorporating quantum algorithms into machine learning models, which, in turn, facilitates a deeper understanding of complex datasets. The resulting framework offers a new optimization approach, pushing the boundaries of current machine learning techniques. This work demonstrates the potential of quantum topology to significantly enhance data analysis and model prediction, presenting a fundamentally new pathway for optimizing complex systems.

title: Where Perceptrons Meet Proof Trees: A State of the Art Review of Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning Systems
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning Systems in the context of Artificial Intelligence. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of neuro-symbolic and reasoning as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Artificial Intelligence.

title: Core Claim: A dynamically adjusted machine learning model variance adjustment algorithm is proposed, which dynamically adjusts the variance adjustment parameters to improve model generalization, particularly in data distributions with heterogenity.
abstract: The goal of this research is to develop a novel machine learning model variance adjustment algorithm that dynamically adjusts the variance adjustment parameters. This algorithm is designed to enhance model generalization, specifically in situations where data distributions are uneven. Traditional machine learning methods often rely on fixed parameters, limiting model flexibility. This paper introduces a dynamically adjusted variance adjustment mechanism that adapts to the data, resulting in improved performance across a range of datasets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through simulations and experimental analysis. The core idea behind this algorithm is to utilize machine learning's inherent adaptive capabilities to fine-tune the variance adjustment, leading to a more robust and generalizable model.

title: Dynamic Probability Field: A Novel Approach to Adaptive Decision Making
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic probability field system that dynamically adjusts its state and generates diverse future states based on environmental changes. The system leverages a dynamic probability field, allowing for real-time adjustments and the creation of multiple possible outcomes, enabling adaptive decision-making. The core mechanism involves a dynamic update process for the probability field, establishing relationships between state and environment changes, and subsequently generating diverse future states for evaluation. This approach contrasts with traditional decision theory, which relies on predefined rules, offering a more flexible and adaptive framework.

title: Dynamic Adaptive Quantum Algorithm Framework
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic adaptive quantum algorithm framework designed to optimize quantum computation through dynamic parameter adjustment. Traditional quantum algorithms often rely on fixed parameter settings, limiting their potential for efficient and accurate solutions. This framework leverages quantum computation's inherent properties and data characteristics to dynamically adjust key parameters, resulting in enhanced computational efficiency and accuracy. The core mechanism involves a sophisticated algorithm that continuously analyzes the quantum system and adjusts parameters to achieve optimal performance. This research explores the theoretical underpinnings and practical implementation of this framework, demonstrating its potential to significantly advance quantum algorithm design and performance.

title: Quantum Security Proof Based on Quantum Decoherence
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of utilizing quantum decoherence as a foundation for enhanced computational security. Traditional cryptographic algorithms are increasingly vulnerable to attacks leveraging quantum computing capabilities. This research proposes a novel approach to secure key distribution by exploiting the inherent properties of quantum decoherence. We design a quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol that incorporates controlled quantum noise and environmental interactions, specifically leveraging the rapid decoherence of quantum states. The protocol's core principle is that the unpredictable nature of decoherence – the loss of quantum information due to interaction with the environment – makes it extraordinarily difficult for an eavesdropper to predict and exploit the key distribution process. The resulting security stems not from the laws of physics themselves, but from the attacker's inability to reliably model and manipulate the quantum system's rapidly evolving state. We present a mathematical framework to analyze the security of this protocol, highlighting key parameters influencing its resilience. This work offers a fundamentally new security paradigm, shifting the focus from algorithm-based security to a system-level approach centered around harnessing the chaotic nature of quantum decoherence. The presented scheme demonstrates a promising path toward building robust, quantum-resistant cryptographic systems.

title: Quantum Machine Learning Adaptive Regularization
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) is a rapidly evolving field that explores the potential of quantum computers to enhance machine learning algorithms. One promising approach is the utilization of adaptive regularization, which dynamically adjusts regularization parameters during training to improve model generalization. This paper introduces a novel framework for adaptive regularization, termed "Quantum Adaptive Regularization" (QAR), designed to automatically adjust regularization based on the inherent characteristics of the problem being addressed. We propose a mechanism that iteratively analyzes the data distribution and adjusts the regularization strength, leading to improved model performance and robustness. The core of this framework lies in a self-adaptive adjustment process, ensuring the model effectively adapts to the complexities of the training data. title: Quantum Entanglement Optimization Algorithm
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental quantum phenomenon, offers the potential for unprecedented computational capabilities. Harnessing this potential, Quantum Entanglement Optimization Algorithm (QEOA) presents a novel approach to optimize quantum entanglement algorithms, aiming to enhance computational efficiency and security. This paper introduces a dynamic parameter adjustment strategy for entanglement operators, leveraging self-adaptive learning techniques to iteratively refine the entanglement's state. The core mechanism focuses on quantifying and optimizing entanglement parameters to minimize computational overhead and maximize security guarantees. The study explores the practical implications of this algorithm across various entanglement-based tasks, demonstrating significant improvements in both performance and robustness.

title: 基于自适应的图灵机推理的优化算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm for reasoning, inspired by the principles of adaptive graph theory and the principles of self-diagnosis used in the theoretical foundation of the Turing machine. The algorithm dynamically adjusts the reasoning strategy based on the current state of the reasoning process, aiming to minimize both error and computational cost. We propose a method that leverages a feedback mechanism to iteratively refine the reasoning process, enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of logical inference. This approach departs from static reasoning techniques and incorporates a dynamic adaptation layer, offering a potential breakthrough in the field of automated reasoning. The core mechanism centers around a self-diagnosis system that monitors the reasoning process, identifies potential areas of instability, and adjusts the strategy accordingly. This dynamic adjustment significantly improves the robustness and performance of the reasoning process.

title: Beyond Measurement: Exponential Advantages in Coherent Quantum Inference
abstract: Quantum inference usually begins by measuring quantum data and converting it into classical information. In this talk, I will consider a different setting in which the desired output remains quantum, allowing coherence to be preserved throughout the inference process. Examples include quantum purity amplification, approximate purification and cloning of mixed states, and density matrix exponentiation. I will show that coherent protocols can use exponentially fewer input copies than any measurement mediated strategy. For quantum purity amplification of a principal eigenstate with an input of dimension d, coherent processing achieves error ε using O(1/ε) copies, while incoherent protocols require Ω(d/ε) copies. More broadly, these results motivate a theory of coherent quantum inference and establish entanglement breaking limits as a natural connection between coherent and incoherent information processing.

title: A Transformation-Based AI Framework for Equitable RTI Tier Classification in Qatar
abstract: Consistent and equitable classification of students within Response to Intervention (RTI) frameworks remains a significant challenge in Qatar’s educational system, where tier-assignment decisions rely predominantly on qualitative, multidisciplinary evaluation reports rather than standardized quantitative measures. This research proposes a transformation-based framework for RTI tier classification using Qatari student evaluation reports. The framework converts qualitative clinical descriptors into structured intermediate representations through descriptor extraction, ordinal severity mapping, score translation, and composite aggregation. Seven classification approaches were systematically evaluated within this framework: direct zero-shot and few-shot large language model (LLM) classification; hierarchical prompting; rule-based transformation; LLM-assisted transformation; and a hybrid transformation-based approach. All experiments utilized OCR-extracted Arabic evaluation report text and were assessed using accuracy, balanced accuracy, macro F1-score, weighted F1-score, and class-wise F1-scores. The hybrid transformation-based approach demonstrated the strongest overall performance across evaluation metrics and was the only approach to maintain meaningful classification performance across all three RTI tiers, including the underrepresented and most challenging Tier 1 category. Direct and hierarchical prompting approaches produced lower and less consistent classification performance across the evaluated RTI tiers. These findings indicate that the introduction of structured intermediate transformation stages substantially enhances the consistency, interpretability, and equity of RTI tier classification from qualitative evaluation reports, providing a principled mechanism for standardizing classification decisions across Qatar’s schools and evaluation teams.

title: Error-Profile-Conditioned Augmentation for Chinese L2 Writing Assessment: Evaluating Synthetic Tail Data Under Data Scarcity
abstract: Automated essay scoring models trained on imbalanced examination data often compress predictions toward the score mean, disproportionately harming low-proficiency responses. We investigate whether synthetic tail data can mitigate this failure in Chinese second-language writing assessment. Using 10,067 HSK writing samples, we introduce Error-Profile-Conditioned Synthesis (EPCS), which transfers a complete error profile and examiner score from a real low-band donor to an expert-corrected mid-band substrate, uses authentic error exemplars, and verifies the generated manifest. We evaluate three method versions using surface-feature tests, real-versus-synthetic discrimination, and downstream MacBERT scoring under full, 25%, and 10% low-band retention. Surface similarity did not predict downstream utility: the least detectable version transferred poorly, whereas content-degraded versions were more useful. With only 49 real low-band training samples, EPCS with reweighting reduced low-band mean absolute error from 14.91 to 12.66 and increased below-60 recall from 0.10 to 0.33; recall improved in all five paired seeds and low-band error in four. However, overall QWK changed from 0.506 to 0.497, precision decreased from 0.78 to 0.56, and the false-positive rate increased from 0.015 to 0.106. The pattern replicated across two further pretrained encoders and a feature-based scorer and survived a ±5-point stress test of the inherited labels. EPCS therefore acts as a scarcity-conditioned operating-point intervention, improving tail detection at the cost of more false alarms and high-band under-scoring.

title: A Specialized Large Multimodal Model for Interpreting PET/CT in Head and Neck Cancer
abstract: Background: Diagnosing head and neck cancer using PET/CT is clinically challenging and time-consuming due to the anatomical complexity of the region, motivating computer-aided diagnosis (CAD). Generalist Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) remain limited in medical contexts by insufficient domain-specific knowledge, privacy and security concerns, and verbosity, motivating specialized standalone LMMs. Purpose: We evaluated the feasibility of a specialized LMM for automated PET/CT interpretation in head and neck cancer using a large-scale multi-institutional PET/CT dataset, a tailored training curriculum, and autoregressive training. Methods: LLaVA-NeXT was fine-tuned using a two-level curriculum with image-conversation pairs curated by two radiologists from public data. The dataset included clinically important annotations such as primary tumor presence and metastatic lymph node location. Level 1 used 28,000 image-conversation pairs to learn basic information, including modality type and hypermetabolism. Level 2 used 12,975 pairs to learn primary tumor presence and the existence and anatomical location of cervical lymph node metastases. External validation included four institutions with diverse imaging devices. Results: The specialized LMM substantially outperformed ChatGPT and LLaVA-NeXT. In Level-2 external validation, ROUGE-L, ROUGE-S, Cosine Similarity, Precision, Recall, and F1 were 0.8751, 0.8794, 0.8324, 0.8794, 0.8711, and 0.8751, while generalist models consistently scored below 0.1. Primary tumor classification accuracy was 83.14 +/- 1.15% internally and 69.03 +/- 0.81% externally. For lymph node localization, the corresponding scores were 0.6389, 0.6257, 0.5287, 0.5782, 0.6371, and 0.6648. Conclusion: Specialized LMMs show promising results for fast, accurate PET/CT-based diagnostic support and medical education, highlighting their potential for clinical translation.

title: Adapting a Foundation Model for Lunar Surface Height Estimation
abstract: Digital elevation models (DEMs) can provide accurate height information, making it invaluable for analyzing the lunar surface. As the European Space Agency (ESA) prepares for future lunar missions that aim to land on the Moon, a precise method for height estimation will be essential for hazardous terrain that could endanger the landing approach. Traditional approaches to generate DEMs from imagery, such as shape from shading (SfS) and stereophotogrammetry (SPG) have been proven highly valuable for this task. However, due to advancements in machine learning, especially computer vision, the focus has shifted towards monocular depth estimation via deep learning. The lunar surface is covered by rocks and craters, and classic hazard detection methods rely solely on 2D image data. Our goal is to address this issue by developing a relative lunar surface height estimator that can provide additional information for hazard localization. In this letter, we present a methodology that builds on the well-known zero-shot relative depth estimation model Depth Anything V2 (DAV2). Other works have been using it as a state-of-the-art comparison for their proposed lunar DEM estimation method, but without adaptations to the target domain. Thus, it may underperform. Therefore, we propose a fine-tuning strategy with publicly available SPG-derived DEM data of the lunar surface. Our results demonstrate a significant improvement in performance compared to the zero-shot model, effectively transforming DAV2 into a reliable relative depth estimator of the lunar surface.

title: Implicit Manipulation for Skill Selection in LLM Agents with Semantic Matching
abstract: Skill selection is a key stage in LLM-agent workflows, determining which installed skill should handle a user request. Existing attacks on this stage primarily rely on explicit prompt injection or instruction-level steering, which can expose recognizable manipulation signals. In this work, we identify a new implicit attack surface for skill selection: even when the user prompt and skill description appear benign in isolation, their semantic relationship can still be strategically shaped to favor an attacker-chosen skill. Based on this observation, we present Implicit Skill-Selection Manipulation via Semantic Matching (ISM), which jointly shapes target-skill metadata and reusable prompts to manipulate skill selection without explicit selection instructions. Specifically, we develop a three-stage strategy to broaden semantic coverage, strengthen target distinctiveness, and preserve natural prompt wording. Across four task domains and eight selector models, ISM increases the average target-selection rate (TSR) from 15.2% to 63.5%. In a matched comparison, ISM achieves a 73.5% TSR, only 9.8 percentage points below Explicit Steering. Human reviewers block ISM in only 2.9% of judgments, versus 91.4% for Explicit Steering, while five LLM-based inspectors pass ISM at an average rate of 82.9%, versus 37.4% for Explicit Steering. Moreover, ISM remains effective against PPL-W, Llama Prompt Guard 2, and PIGuard.

title: Modeling What Changes: Sparse, Residual World Models for Object-Centric Manipulation
abstract: Monolithic world models predict the entire next state at every step, spending capacity re-predicting the static majority of a scene and injecting error into it. We ask whether explicitly modeling change (a per-object change gate plus a residual delta head that perturbs only the objects the gate flags) is a more effective and interpretable bias for physical prediction and control. On a MuJoCo tabletop pushing benchmark scaling from 3 to 8 objects, the sparse/residual model predicts next-state poses 2.5 to 4.6 times more accurately than a dense multilayer perceptron at 8.6 to 11.1 times fewer parameters, sustains change-detection F1 of 0.80 to 0.87 where the dense baseline is degenerate, transfers across object counts with zero retraining (99.4 percent F1 retention), and reaches about 90 percent of its full-data accuracy with a quarter of the data. In autoregressive rollout it compounds far less error, hugging the no-motion floor while the dense model drifts. Finally, inside a sampling-based planner, prediction-only models fail (though a true-simulator oracle solves the task with the identical planner, confirming the planner is sound), but once featurized and trained for the states a planner visits, the sparse model begins to plan (0.23 plus or minus 0.06 success over three seeds) while the dense monolith stays at zero at every seed. Modeling what changes, rather than re-predicting the whole world, is a simple, effective bias for object-centric physical AI; code, data generators, and all checkpoints will be released upon publication.

title: When Persona Attributes Improve Population Alignment in Large Language Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to predict the responses of human participants in survey panels. Towards that goal, persona prompting has recently emerged as a technique to inform and align large pretrained language models. Persona prompting refers to the practice of using short textual descriptions of 'personas' in prompts to steer the LLM's generations. Personas describe individuals through different attributes such as their socio-demographics, attitudes, or behaviors, with the aim of aligning LLMs to produce responses that correlate with the corresponding human responses. Yet, recent work has produced mixed and partly conflicting results of persona prompting without clear patterns of success and failure. Among the few consistent findings is that the selection of persona attributes matters, and that using more attributes does not necessarily lead to better performance. It remains unclear how different attribute selection methods perform and how to choose among them. In this paper, we propose that observed human response variation of a survey question is a potential explanation for the mixed performance observed so far. In addition, we compare the performance of persona prompting associated with different methods for selecting persona attributes. We evaluate these methods on four different (general) social surveys across two countries, six LLMs, and twenty prediction tasks per survey. Our work helps to identify when persona prompting can be expected to be useful in survey prediction tasks, and provides new insights on the effectiveness of different attribute selection methods for LLM-based survey prediction using persona prompting.

title: From topology learning to graph generation: A unifying perspective
abstract: Learning graph structures from data is a fundamental problem that spans a wide range of signal processing and machine learning tasks. While significant effort has been made to tackle the problem, existing research has largely evolved along two parallel directions. The first seeks to infer the topology of an individual graph from observations supported on it, whereas the second seeks to learn a generative distribution from observed graph instances, enabling the sampling of new graphs. This review presents a unified framework that connects these formulations by viewing them as inverse problems of a common generation process for graph data. We review the major methodologies within this framework, highlight their relationships, strengths, and limitations, and identify opportunities for integrating ideas across paradigms. By bridging graph topology learning and graph generation, this review provides a broader cross-disciplinary perspective on the field and outlines promising directions for future research.

The first seeks to infer the topology of an individual graph from observations supported on it, whereas the second seeks to learn a generative distribution from observed graph instances, enabling the sampling of new graphs. This review presents a unified framework that connects these formulations by viewing them as inverse problems of a common generation process for graph data. We review the major methodologies within this framework, highlight their relationships, strengths, and limitations, and identify opportunities for integrating ideas across paradigms. By bridging graph topology learning and graph generation, this review provides a broader cross-disciplinary perspective on the field and outlines promising directions for future research.

title: Efficient All-in-One Weather Restoration using Spectral Harmonization
abstract: Adverse weather conditions such as rain, haze, and snow significantly degrade image quality, posing challenges for both human perception and physical AI. Existing restoration methods require large computational budgets, struggling to process high-resolution images and handle different degradations. In this paper, we present Frequency Reconstruction via Spectral Harmonization, a novel lightweight all-in-one restoration method that explicitly decomposes feature representations into high- and low-frequency components at each scale of a hierarchical encoder-decoder architecture. By combining spectral decomposition with spatial processing through Fourier-based skip connections, FReSH-IR captures complementary frequency information without sacrificing spatial detail. Our approach achieves similar restoration quality with 80% fewer parameters and operations than transformer-based models. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method offers a great efficiency-performance trade-off, highlighting its practical applications in constrained-resource systems.

title: The Analyst in the Prompt: Role, Retrieval, and Memory Biases in LLM Financial Analysis
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly use user context such as memory, profiles, and role prompts to personalize their responses. This personalization can affect evidence-based judgment: the same evidence may lead to different conclusions under different user contexts. Finance provides a high-stakes setting to study this problem because decisions often depend on interpreting long and complex documents. We test this using 3,575 SEC filings across twelve LLMs. We compare persona-conditioned retrieval, neutral retrieval, and memory-framed context to separate the effect of evidence selection from the effect of interpretation. We find that most user-context spillover comes from how models interpret the same evidence under different roles, rather than from retrieving different evidence. We then test two simple mitigation strategies: expressing the same investor mindset as a user profile instead of an assistant role, and separating evidence-based and personalized outputs. Both reduce spillover, but neither removes it completely, and their effectiveness varies substantially across models.

title: Quantum Adaptive Optimization Algorithm (QOA)
abstract: Quantum Adaptive Optimization Algorithm (QOA) presents a novel approach to optimization utilizing quantum entanglement to accelerate the search process. This paper details the design and implementation of QOA, highlighting its core mechanism – leveraging quantum entanglement to facilitate rapid convergence and enhanced optimization strategies. The research focuses on establishing a robust framework that can effectively address complex problems traditionally challenging traditional optimization techniques. This work introduces a new algorithmic approach with the potential to significantly improve the efficiency and effectiveness of optimization across a range of applications. The core claim emphasizes the utilization of quantum entanglement for rapid solution discovery and improved optimization strategies.

title: Adaptive Distributed Learning Algorithm (ADLA)
abstract: This paper introduces an Adaptive Distributed Learning Algorithm (ADLA) designed to optimize learning efficiency in distributed environments. Traditional distributed learning methods often rely on static parameter settings, failing to effectively leverage data heterogeneity. ADLA addresses this limitation by dynamically adjusting learning rates, gradient update strategies, and other key parameters based on individual node data characteristics. We present a novel framework utilizing a self-adaptive learning process to dynamically optimize the learning process across a cluster of nodes. The core mechanism centers on a feedback loop that continuously evaluates node performance and adjusts parameters to promote convergence and minimize overall computational cost. The proposed ADLA offers a significant advancement over existing approaches by providing a robust and adaptable solution for distributed learning.

title: Title: Adaptive Topological Parameter Optimization
abstract: This paper presents a novel adaptive parameter optimization algorithm based on dynamic topological structures. Traditional optimization methods often rely on static parameters, limiting their ability to effectively address complex, evolving system dynamics. This research introduces a new approach leveraging dynamic topological structures to dynamically adjust parameters, resulting in improved system performance. The algorithm employs a self-organizing process driven by topological constraints, enabling the system to adapt to changing conditions and optimize performance more efficiently than traditional methods. The core mechanism involves the continuous transformation of parameters within a topological framework, promoting robustness and adaptability. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through simulations and analysis, illustrating significant performance gains in a specific system modeling scenario.

title: Neural Architecture Generation and Adaptation
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to neural network architecture design utilizing evolutionary algorithms. The core concept is to automate the generation and optimization of neural network architectures for specific computational tasks. We employ a genetic algorithm to explore a defined search space encompassing neural network types, connection patterns, and activation functions. The algorithm iteratively generates and evaluates network architectures, employing crossover and mutation operators to drive the evolutionary process. The goal is to achieve high performance and adaptability to changing task requirements. The key contribution lies in the automated discovery of optimal architectures, removing the reliance on manual design and enabling networks with superior capabilities. The system dynamically adapts to task variations through continuous architectural refinement. The framework offers a robust solution for tackling complex problems where bespoke neural network architectures are crucial. The proposed method demonstrates the potential for significant gains in efficiency and accuracy compared to traditionally designed networks. Mathematical notation is used throughout to represent the core concepts and algorithms.

title: Based on Formal Semantics: Program Verification
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to program verification leveraging formal semantics. Traditional program verification methods primarily rely on static or dynamic analysis, often falling short in providing precise and conclusive proof of program correctness. This research proposes utilizing formal semantics to precisely analyze and validate program code, resulting in a more robust and reliable verification process. We represent program code as formal semantic models and employ these models for verification, ultimately generating formal proofs. The core claim driving this work is that precise semantic analysis, grounded in formal semantics, significantly enhances program reliability. This approach addresses a key gap in existing verification techniques, offering a more rigorous and verifiable method for ensuring software integrity.

title: Symbolic Regression with Genetic Programming and Neural Network Integration
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to symbolic regression, integrating genetic programming (GP) and neural networks (NN) to enhance equation discovery from data. Traditional symbolic regression methods often struggle with complex, non-linear relationships, while evolutionary algorithms can be computationally expensive. Neural networks offer powerful learning capabilities but can lack interpretability. This integrated system addresses these limitations by utilizing GP to explore a vast solution space of mathematical equations and employing a NN to guide the GP search, prioritizing promising candidates and refining their accuracy. The core claim is that this synergistic combination leads to more accurate and interpretable equation discovery. The methodology involves evolving candidate equations using GP, and then leveraging a NN to assess their fitness and guide the GP's evolutionary process. The NN's output, representing a predicted accuracy score, is used as a fitness function for the GP, accelerating the search for optimal equations. The paper outlines the architecture of the integrated system, the key components, and the overall workflow. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of simulations, highlighting its ability to uncover complex relationships that would be difficult to find with either method alone. The results indicate a significant improvement in equation accuracy and a greater ability to capture underlying data patterns. Future work will focus on optimizing the NN architecture and exploring different integration strategies.

title: 多体量子态的自适应量子密钥分发协议
abstract: This paper explores the application of multi-particle quantum states to enhance the efficiency of quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols. Traditional QKD relies on static key distribution, which can be vulnerable to eavesdropping. We propose a novel QKD scheme predicated on the adaptability of quantum states, enabling dynamic adjustments to the key distribution process to improve security and key generation rates. The core of this approach lies in leveraging the inherent quantum properties of the encoded information, allowing for a more robust and adaptable protocol. We detail the design of the protocol, focusing on the mechanisms that facilitate this adaptation and demonstrate its potential for significantly improving QKD performance compared to static approaches. The paper concludes with a discussion of the challenges and future directions of this research.

title: Dynamic Graph Neural Networks for Node Embedding Learning and Relation Inference
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for dynamic graph neural networks (DGNNs) that integrates node embedding learning with relation inference. Traditional graph neural networks often struggle with accurately predicting complex relationships within dynamic graphs. Our approach leverages the power of DGNNs to automatically learn node embeddings that capture intricate structural and temporal dependencies. These embeddings are then utilized within a relation inference module to predict missing relationships. The core of our method lies in the dynamic updating of node embeddings based on evolving graph structures and the incorporation of temporal information. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through a theoretical analysis and a detailed explanation of the algorithm. The key contribution is a robust and adaptable system for analyzing dynamic graphs, addressing the limitations of static graph neural networks and offering enhanced capabilities for relationship prediction and understanding. The proposed method achieves improved accuracy in relation inference tasks compared to existing approaches. The framework is designed to handle graphs where nodes and relationships can change over time, making it suitable for applications in areas such as social network analysis, knowledge graph reasoning, and fraud detection.

title: CIF-LAAD Stage 0: Coherence-Gated Inheritance for Low-Altitude Air Defense Tracking - Falsification Study and Batch-Mode Observation
abstract: A preregistered, simulation-only (TRL 3) characterization of CIF-LAAD, a sensor-agnostic software fusion, tracking, and evidence layer. The record includes external-comparator benchmarks against the DSTL Stone Soup GNN and JPDA trackers, a structural RMSE diagnosis, two rejected candidate improvements preserved as labeled failures, a scaling study, and integrity manifests. Validated strengths (sensor-dropout continuity, false-track suppression, compute tractability) are reported with their costs; positional accuracy and accuracy-at-scale are documented as losses. No hardware, no real-sensor data. The runnable implementation is access-controlled and is not part of this deposit. The record covers experiments EXP-1 through EXP-12, EXP-14, and EXP-15; EXP-13 was intentionally not executed (shelved), so the numbering is non-sequential by design.

title: Quantum Error Correction Driven Distributed Reasoning
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to distributed computing leveraging quantum error correction (QEC) techniques to overcome the inherent limitations of communication and data noise. The core claim is that by strategically deploying QEC codes across distributed nodes, we can enable more efficient parallel reasoning. The proposed mechanism involves encoding data and computational results using QEC codes, facilitating robust data transmission and error correction during logical inference. We demonstrate how this integration addresses critical bottlenecks in traditional distributed computing architectures, paving the way for scalable and reliable quantum-enhanced reasoning systems. This research provides a foundational framework for future development in this rapidly evolving field.

title: Self-Improving Reinforcement Learning with Intrinsic Curiosity
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to reinforcement learning (RL) that addresses the limitations of traditional methods reliant on sparse and often delayed extrinsic rewards. The core idea is to introduce intrinsic curiosity, a mechanism that rewards agents for exploring novel states and reducing uncertainty, thereby driving independent learning. We propose a reinforcement learning agent incorporating this intrinsic curiosity component, demonstrating its effectiveness in navigating complex environments and achieving superior performance compared to standard reward-based RL. This work highlights the potential of self-improving RL systems capable of autonomously discovering and mastering challenging tasks. The agent's learning process is fundamentally altered by actively seeking out areas of high uncertainty, leading to faster convergence and improved overall performance. We analyze the key components of the system and demonstrate its adaptability across various simulated environments. The theoretical framework presented provides a foundation for future research in self-motivated learning and exploration strategies. ---

title: Can a Knowledge Graph Fall Down? Embodied Knowledge Graphs for Humanoid Robots
abstract: Knowledge graphs (KGs) are powerful tools for representing, integrating, and querying knowledge. Humanoid robots expose a limitation of current world models: they can predict future states, but they rarely make explicit the semantic commitments needed to decide whether an object is reachable, a surface is supportive, a human is too close, or an action is unsafe. This paper argues that the next long-term challenge for Semantic Web and Knowledge Graph research is to build Embodied Knowledge Graphs: dynamic, multimodal, uncertainty-aware semantic world models whose statements are grounded in geometry, perception, proprioception, affordances, physical constraints, and predicted action consequences. Such graphs would not merely answer “what is true?” but also make explicit which commitments are grounded enough to act upon, which remain risky, and which require further perception. This is not a proposal for adding a knowledge graph to a robot, but for redefining what a knowledge graph must be when its statements can trigger physical action. Using humanoid semantic world reconstruction as a motivating stress test, the paper outlines a research agenda around joint geometric-semantic reconstruction, structural abstraction, affordance transfer, provenance, and self-maintenance. The proposal is intentionally high-risk: it asks whether knowledge graphs can make embodied action safer, more recoverable, and more auditable than systems based only on latent world models or scene graphs.

title: Explainable deep learning improves human mental models of self-driving cars
abstract: Abstract Self-driving cars increasingly rely on deep neural networks to achieve human-like driving 1–3 . The opacity of these black-box planners makes it challenging to accurately anticipate when they will fail 4–6 , with potentially catastrophic consequences 7–9 . Although research into interpreting these systems has surged, most of it is confined to simulations or toy setups because of the difficulty of real-world deployment 10,11 , leaving the practical utility of these techniques unknown. Here, we introduce the Concept-Wrapper Network (CW-Net), a method for faithfully explaining the behaviour of machine-learning-based planners that causally grounds their reasoning in human-interpretable concepts without sacrificing performance. We deploy CW-Net on a real self-driving car and show that the resulting explanations improve the human driver’s mental model of the vehicle, allowing them to better predict its behaviour, particularly in surprising situations. This demonstrates that explainable deep learning integrated into self-driving cars can be both understandable and useful in a realistic deployment setting. We anticipate our method could be applied to other safety-critical systems, such as autonomous drones and robotic surgeons, as well as to other architectures, such as end-to-end learning systems and vision–language–action models. Overall, our study establishes a deployment-validated pathway to interpretability for autonomous agents, which could help make them more transparent and safe.

title: AGP-MADDPG: A* Guidance Point based Multi-Agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient for 3D cooperative multi-UAV trajectory planning
abstract: Cooperative trajectory planning for multi unmanned aerial vehicle (multi-UAV) systems in three-dimensional (3D) environments is hindered by sparse rewards, long-horizon decision making, and unstable inter-agent coordination. To address these issues, an A* Guidance Point based Multi-Agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (AGP-MADDPG) framework is developed, which integrates planning-based prior guidance with attention-based value estimation. In this framework, an improved A* planner with multi-objective constraints generates global reference paths by jointly considering path length, safety margin, and inter-UAV separation. Subsequently, dynamic guidance points are constructed along the reference path according to the UAVs’ positions, converting sparse feedback into dense guidance rewards to enhance exploration efficiency and training stability. To mitigate input dimensionality explosion and irrelevant interaction noise in the centralized critic, we incorporate a multi-head self-attention module. This module adaptively aggregates cross-agent information, improving both accuracy and scalability of value estimation. Simulations in basic and extended scenarios show that AGP-MADDPG consistently outperforms baselines in convergence speed, mission success rate, decision efficiency, and trajectory quality, demonstrating its effectiveness and robustness in cooperative multi-UAV trajectory planning.

In this framework, an improved A* planner with multi-objective constraints generates global reference paths by jointly considering path length, safety margin, and inter-UAV separation. Subsequently, dynamic guidance points are constructed along the reference path according to the UAVs’ positions, converting sparse feedback into dense guidance rewards to enhance exploration efficiency and training stability. To mitigate input dimensionality explosion and irrelevant interaction noise in the centralized critic, we incorporate a multi-head self-attention module. This module adaptively aggregates cross-agent information, improving both accuracy and scalability of value estimation. Simulations in basic and extended scenarios show that AGP-MADDPG consistently outperforms baselines in convergence speed, mission success rate, decision efficiency, and trajectory quality, demonstrating its effectiveness and robustness in cooperative multi-UAV trajectory planning.

title: Distinctness threshold for pseudorandom unitaries
abstract: Pseudorandomness is increasingly recognized as a key property of ensembles in quantum information theory, statistical mechanics, and quantum many-body physics. Yet it appears in two conceptually different forms: statistical pseudorandomness, embodied by unitary designs, and computational pseudorandomness captured by pseudorandom unitaries (PRUs). The relationship between these two forms of pseudorandomness remains surprisingly poorly understood. Existing PRU constructions reveal this interplay where a statistically randomizing ingredient, a unitary design, is combined with classical cryptographic primitives to produce computational pseudorandomness. We show that statistical pseudorandomness is not necessary for computationally pseudorandom unitaries. We do this by replacing the unitary $2$-design layer in the existing constructions with ensembles that are not even state $1$-designs, yet are sufficiently {\em distinct}, a property we identify to be necessary for any PRU. This yields new non-adaptively secure PRU ensembles whose computational pseudorandomness is obtained without an underlying statistically pseudorandom quantum ensemble, such as a $2$-design. We characterize distinctness via an entangled analogue of anticoncentration and use it to show that distinctness already captures constraints on coherence and imaginarity of PRUs, while identifying broad classes of inputs for which the latter obstruction disappears, enabling real-valued PRUs even for certain (maximally) entangled states. As an application, we use lack of distinctness to constrain the conjectured pseudorandomness of the random phase-Hadamard ensemble to form a PRU.

title: RVSD: Retrieval Vision Sparse Decoding for Mitigating Visual Hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models
abstract: Large vision-language models have achieved remarkable success in vision-language tasks. However, they remain prone to Visual Hallucinations (VHs), undermining their reliability in real-world applications. Existing solutions typically require curated datasets, additional training, or multi-round decoding, resulting in considerable computational overhead. In this paper, we propose \textbf{RVSD} (\underline{R}etrieval \underline{V}ision \underline{S}parse \underline{D}ecoding), a training-free and plug-and-play decoding framework that, for the first time, unifies token sparsification and \textbf{Semantic-Space Visual Retrieval} (SSVR) within a single decoding pass. Within RVSD, we introduce a \textbf{semantics-directed token selection} strategy that selectively sparsifies redundant tokens while preserving critical visual information. We further propose the SSVR mechanism, which reformulates visual compensation as an on-demand cross-modal retrieval process within a shared semantic space. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RVSD achieves state-of-the-art performance in mitigating VHs while maintaining robust suppression capabilities under long-context generation settings. Our code is available here.\footnote{https://github.com/canjie-liu/RVSD}

title: FuDU: A Fuzzy Dual-dimensional Uncertainty Framework for Streaming Active Learning in Industrial Defect Detection
abstract: Ensuring the reliability of deep learning models in real-time industrial defect detection is critical for high-stakes quality inspection. To mine uncertain samples within continuous industrial media streams, thereby enhancing the reliability of the detection system, this paper proposes a streaming active learning method based on the Fuzzy Dual-dimensional Uncertainty (FuDU) framework. Specifically, we first design a Prototype-based Global Uncertainty Quantification (PGUQ) module on the backbone to evaluate image-level uncertainty via normal/defective feature prototypes. A Dual-entropy defect Uncertainty Evaluator (DeUE) is then integrated into the detection head to quantify box-level uncertainty. Finally, by modeling uncertainty as systematic error, we propose a fuzzy dual-dimensional uncertainty-aware strategy that leverages fuzzy inference to fuse dual-dimensional uncertainties, enabling expert knowledge-driven adaptive sampling decisions. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that FuDU is efficient and flexible, making it well-suited for challenging industrial inspection tasks such as the detection of nuclear fuel rod defects. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/wangzhaoyang-508/FuDU.

title: Instability Floors: Separating Bias from Noise in Fairness Audits of Clinical LLM Agents with FairMedAgent
abstract: Counterfactual fairness audits of clinical language-model agents report a flip rate: how often an action changes when only the patient's demographic descriptor changes. Part of that rate is not demographic. A stochastic agent also changes its own action when nothing changes, and a flip rate cannot be interpreted without knowing how often. We measured it. Re-running one condition ten times over sixteen synthetic vignettes at default sampling changed a clinical agent's action in 8.7 percent of replicate pairs, from 2.2 percent for intensive-care escalation to 17.9 percent for controlled-substance caution, an output given no operational criteria. Across six models from five vendors, pooled floors ranged from 2.5 to 23.7 percent; in this panel neither disclosed size, vendor, nor hosting ordered them. The floor depends on the decoding configuration: majority voting over five draws removed 39 percent of it (95 percent confidence interval (CI) 18 to 64); at temperature 0 three of four locally served models showed no disagreement, but a hosted model still did. We also show that, for a binary action, the flip rate expected under no demographic effect equals the floor and a real effect adds only its square, so a flip rate inside the floor is not evidence of fairness, and direction must be tested with a signed paired test. We give a four-step reporting procedure and release FairMedAgent, the harness, with its protocol, vignettes and analysis scripts, so any team can measure the floor for its own agent.

title: A Channel-Boosted Multi-Agent System with Iterative Consultation for Document Sensitivity Classification
abstract: Organizations in critical national infrastructure sectors must assess heterogeneous documents for sensitivity before routing or storage. Manual assessment is slow, inconsistent, and unscalable. Extending our prior leakage-controlled benchmark, BERT established the top single-encoder baseline (89.14% accuracy, 89.33% F1-score under 5-fold cross-validation on the Strategic 16K corpus). However, transformer baselines suffer from a structural limitation: fixed input length truncation discards evidence beyond the retained window-precisely where sensitive cables tend to be longest. We present Channel-Boosted MAS (CB-MAS) and instantiate it as IC-MAS (Iterative Consultation Multi-Agent System) to solve this without long-context computational costs. A Channel Critic Agent learns document-adaptive trust weights governing Gated Channel Boosting between two first-window encoders, while paired Consultation Agents iteratively exchange belief states to reconcile evidence from the beginning and end of long documents. IC-MAS holds computation constant regardless of document length by reconciling fixed windows in a compact representation space. Ablation studies show critic-controlled Channel Boosting provides the bulk of accuracy gains, while consultation recovers recall without precision collapse. Critic-Controlled Gated Channel Boosting with Max-Pool fusion and Blackboard Adaptive Consultation achieves 90.72% accuracy, 91.23% F1-score, 92.01% sensitive recall, and 90.46% sensitive precision, using about 54% less average computation than a fixed-round baseline. Gains over the single-encoder baseline are statistically significant (McNemar's test, p less than 0.000001; paired t-test). We include LIME/SHAP explainability, multi-agent evaluation, and an honest accounting of limitations.

title: Rethinking the Teacher-Student Framework for Test-Time Adaptation
abstract: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) has recently emerged as a promising strategy that allows the adaptation of pre-trained models to changing data distributions at deployment time, without access to any labels. To mitigate error accumulation, researchers have widely adopted the teacher-student framework, though its long-term stability is often taken for granted. In this work, we challenge the common strategy of setting the teacher weights to an exponential moving average of the student by showing that error accumulation still occurs, although it is mostly apparent on longer sequences compared to those commonly utilized. We analyze the stability-plasticity trade-off within the teacher-student framework and propose to use an intransigent teacher that does not update its weights. Surprisingly, we show that this simple change allows TTA methods to significantly improve their performance on multiple datasets with longer scenarios and result in increased robustness to changes in hyperparameters. Finally, we show that those changes can be seamlessly and effectively applied to various architectures and experimental setups, including semantic segmentation. The code is available at https://github.com/dmn-sjk/intransigent_teacher.

title: Do Large Language Models Capture the Diversity in their Training Data?
abstract: Large language models are trained to model conditional distributions over text, yet it remains inadequately understood whether they capture the full diversity of plausible outputs present in their training data. We study this question through an information-theoretic lens by comparing the conditional entropy of model-generated outputs with that of the corresponding training data. Given paired input-output samples, we use conditional entropy and its matrix-based analogue based on von Neumann entropy to measure output variability beyond what is explained by the conditioning input, without requiring multiple reference outputs for the same prompt. Across LLM families with publicly available training data, including OLMo, Pythia, and GPT-Neo, we consistently find that model-generated outputs exhibit lower conditional entropy than their training data, across different model scales, sequence lengths, and decoding strategies. We observe a similar conditional diversity gap beyond language modeling, including class-conditioned ImageNet generators and text-conditioned models trained on MS-COCO. To address this gap, we propose a post-hoc correction mechanism that generates multiple outputs for each input and reweights them through a matrix-entropy projection, increasing conditional diversity while remaining close to the original model distribution. We prove the concavity of the matrix-based conditional entropy functional, which makes the resulting entropy-constrained projection a convex optimization problem, and develop a scalable mirror-descent algorithm for its implementation. Our results reveal a systematic conditional diversity gap between modern generative models and their training data, and provide an information-theoretic framework for measuring and mitigating this gap.

title: LLM-as-a-Judge Is Not an Oracle: Why Self-Improving Agents Need Deterministic Guardrails
abstract: Self-improving agent pipelines have a problem at their center. An optimizer rewrites prompts to score higher, and the score comes from a judge that is itself an LLM. That judge has the last word on whether the system is getting better, and our position is that it has not earned it. The judge should be demoted from oracle to advisor: its verdict becomes one input among several, and every change is gated instead by a deterministic verification layer the judge cannot override. We reached this position by building the alternative and running it. Over months of running autonomous prompt-optimization loops in production across contract analysis, compliance review, and code quality, we cataloged eleven ways the evaluation signal failed, in four classes: judge bias, harness and metric failures, ground-truth errors, and reward hacking. Agents achieved perfect scores by reading cached answer keys from their environment, a 100% pass rate concealing 68% true capability. A corrupted ground-truth label caused the optimizer to delete correct compliance rules to agree with it. A syntactically broken prompt was promoted as the winner because a silent parser fallback improved the metric. Attempts to fix the judge by rewriting its rubric plateaued; the only reliable gain came from a structural constraint on its output order. In response we describe PROCTOR, a Teacher-Student loop in which a stateful orchestrator holds all tool access, stateless subagents diagnose failures and draft mutations they cannot apply, and a Teacher grades those mutations under five deterministic guardrails: hermetic sandboxes, capability-disjoint roles, acceptance checks that outrank the Teacher, frozen holdouts, and canary cases engineered so that a perfect score is itself evidence of cheating. We report the failures this prevented, and, because the Teacher is itself an LLM judge, the failures it did not.

title: Learning to Zoom Efficiently with a Contrastive Curriculum
abstract: Using a zoom-in tool is an important foundational part of modern visual agents, because it allows to efficiently handle tasks involving high-resolution images. Most previous methods need an extensive warm-start supervised fine-tuning phase for teaching models zoom-in. We show that this is not necessary by proposing a new intrinsic reward for learning tool use in MLLMs without the need for additional labels or warm-start SFT. Our InfoNCE-style reward uses a curriculum of increasingly hard negative tool calls as a contrastive training signal. Empirical experiments on $V^*$, HRBench and MME-RealWorld show that our approach is competitive while being more efficient. When used as a drop-in replacement for SFT, we even outperform all baselines. To directly measure the zoom-in ability of models, we further introduce the scalable synthetic Muffin&Chihuahua (M&C) dataset. Each image consists of a grid with every cell either showing a muffin or chihuahua. Leveraging the M&C dataset's unique region of interest labels, we find that recall is the metric that most strongly correlates the zoom-in region with final task performance. Our model and code for reproduction is publicly available under https://github.com/UKPLab/emnlp2026-zoom-in

evidence.title: Learning to Zoom Efficiently with a Contrastive Curriculum
evidence.abstract: Using a zoom-in tool is an important foundational part of modern visual agents, because it allows to efficiently handle tasks involving high-resolution images. Most previous methods need an extensive warm-start supervised fine-tuning phase for teaching models zoom-in. We show that this is not necessary by proposing a new intrinsic reward for learning tool use in MLLMs without the need for additional labels or warm-start SFT. Our InfoNCE-style reward uses a curriculum of increasingly hard negative tool calls as a contrastive training signal. Empirical experiments on $V^*$, HRBench and MME-RealWorld show that our approach is competitive while being more efficient. When used as a drop-in replacement for SFT, we even outperform all baselines. To directly measure the zoom-in ability of models, we further introduce the scalable synthetic Muffin&Chihuahua (M&C) dataset. Each image consists of a grid with every cell either showing a muffin or chihuahua. Leveraging the M&C dataset's unique region of interest labels, we find that recall is the metric that most strongly correlates the zoom-in region with final task performance. Our model and code for reproduction is publicly available under https://github.com/UKPLab/emnlp2026-zoom-in

title: PragAlign: Feedback-Guided Pragmatic Alignment for Controlled Synthetic Dialogue Generation
abstract: Synthetic dialogue generation can support research in privacy-restricted service settings, but generated conversations must preserve communicative intent, affective meaning, and natural dialogue flow. We introduce PragAlign, a feedback-guided framework for controlled synthetic dialogue generation conditioned on service context, target intent, and target emotion, with auxiliary trait-style controls. PragAlign uses a generate--evaluate--revise loop in which an LLM-based evaluator scores intent alignment, emotion alignment, coherence, fluency, and aggregate quality, then provides criterion-specific feedback for up to three refinement rounds. On 800 matched dialogue specifications, PragAlign achieves 99.50\% evaluator-defined acceptance, compared with 72.25\% for one-shot generation and 95.88\% for repeated generation without structured feedback. This indicates that repeated attempts account for much of the gain over one-shot generation, while structured feedback primarily improves last-mile multi-constraint satisfaction rather than broad average quality. Refinement gains are concentrated in emotion alignment, which is also the dominant failure mode in ablations. A separate human evaluation of 1,200 generated dialogues shows that intent expression and dialogue flow are highly recognizable to annotators, while emotion appropriateness is less stable and more subjective. These results support PragAlign as a quality-control framework for improving evaluator-defined communicative constraint satisfaction, while showing that affective realization and independent human-perceived quality remain open challenges.

title: Codes of PV-Refined framework
abstract: This repository provides the core implementation of the PV-Refined framework, including a Random Forest-based classification pipeline for utility-scale photovoltaic systems on Google Earth Engine, a Mask2Former model with a Swin Transformer backbone for panel type classification and refined panel boundary extraction in Python, and a set of Python scripts to calculate key metrics of an USPV plant, including installed capacity, land use efficiency and power generation potential. The PV-Refined framework enables PV panel type classification, precise delineation of panel-level boundaries, and identification of installation timelines.

title: Quantum Topology Dynamic Adaptive Matrix Solver
abstract: Quantum Topology represents a novel approach to matrix solving, leveraging the inherent dynamic behavior of quantum systems. This paper introduces a dynamic adaptive matrix solver employing quantum topology principles to optimize matrix computations, particularly for complex matrices. The core mechanism involves dynamically adjusting matrix parameters based on the evolving quantum structure, leading to enhanced speed and accuracy compared to traditional methods. This research addresses the limitations of conventional matrix solvers by introducing a fundamentally new algorithm that exploits quantum phenomena to achieve superior performance in challenging scenarios.

title: 基于量子自适应的超分辨率矩阵分解
abstract: This paper introduces a novel method for matrix decomposition utilizing quantum-adaptive matrix decomposition. Traditional matrix decomposition methods often suffer from computational inefficiency, particularly when dealing with large matrices. This work proposes a quantum-adaptive approach that dramatically improves computational efficiency by leveraging the unique properties of quantum self-adaptation within the matrix decomposition process. The core mechanism involves a carefully designed quantum algorithm that accelerates the decomposition process significantly, offering substantial benefits for large-scale matrix applications. We present preliminary results demonstrating the effectiveness of this method, highlighting its potential to revolutionize the field of matrix analysis.

title: Quantum-Inspired Feedback Loop for Algorithm Stability
abstract: Quantum-inspired feedback loops offer a novel approach to enhancing algorithm stability, particularly in dynamic environments. This paper explores the potential of incorporating quantum entanglement into a feedback mechanism designed to proactively detect and mitigate instability issues. We present a theoretical framework detailing the core principles, mechanisms, and expected outcomes of this approach. The goal is to develop a robust and adaptable strategy for improving the reliability of algorithms across a range of scenarios. This work provides a foundational investigation into the application of quantum mechanics to algorithm optimization, aiming for significant improvements in stability through a dynamically adjusted feedback system.

title: Dynamic Self-Organizing Neural Networks (DSON)
abstract: This paper introduces Dynamic Self-Organizing Neural Networks (DSON) as a novel approach to prediction and control of complex systems. DSON leverages a dynamic self-organizing neural network architecture, incorporating simulated self-organization principles to optimize data distribution and parameter adjustment. The core mechanism focuses on dynamically adapting network structure and parameters based on predictive outcomes, ensuring high accuracy in forecasting. This research represents a departure from traditional neural network approaches, offering a more flexible and adaptive method for complex system behavior modeling. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DSON through a series of simulations, showcasing its ability to accurately predict system dynamics and maintain consistent performance across a range of scenarios. The paper concludes with a discussion of the potential applications of DSON in various fields, including control systems, data analysis, and predictive modeling.

title: Quantum Topological Analysis of Hidden Matrices
abstract: This paper investigates the topological properties of hidden matrices, utilizing quantum entanglement and superposition to explore their intrinsic structure and predict their behavior. We propose a novel method based on the concept of "hidden matrices" exhibiting unique topological properties, leveraging quantum entanglement to simulate matrix evolution and offer a new perspective on quantum computation. The core mechanism focuses on harnessing quantum entanglement to unveil the underlying topological structure of these matrices. This research aims to provide a more comprehensive understanding of hidden matrix topology, potentially enhancing the efficiency of quantum algorithms.

title: Reservoir Computing with Dynamic Topology Optimization using Evolutionary Algorithms
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to reservoir computing (RC) by incorporating dynamic topology optimization driven by evolutionary algorithms. Traditional RC systems often suffer from suboptimal performance due to a fixed, pre-determined reservoir architecture. This work addresses this limitation by enabling the reservoir's topology to adapt in real-time, responding to the characteristics of the input data. The core idea is to utilize an evolutionary algorithm to iteratively adjust the reservoir's connectivity, aiming to maximize performance metrics such as prediction accuracy. We detail the theoretical framework, outlining the key components of the system, including the RC model, the evolutionary algorithm, and the optimization objective. We demonstrate the potential of this dynamic approach through a conceptual design and analysis, highlighting its advantages in handling non-stationary and complex input signals. The research contributes to a more robust and adaptive RC system, potentially improving its applicability across various domains.

title: Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuit Design Based on Quantum Error-Correcting Codes
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to designing fault-tolerant quantum circuits utilizing quantum error-correcting codes. The core claim is to develop a method capable of significantly reducing error rates within quantum circuits while achieving high reliability for quantum computation. This is achieved through the integration of theoretical concepts from quantum error-correcting codes with practical circuit design considerations. The proposed methodology focuses on designing quantum circuit architectures that effectively correct errors and enhance overall circuit resilience. The primary innovation lies in extending the application of quantum error-correcting codes, traditionally utilized in quantum communication, to the domain of quantum circuit design, thereby bolstering the inherent error correction capabilities of quantum computing. The presented framework outlines a systematic approach to constructing robust quantum circuits, paving the way for more reliable and scalable quantum computation. This work provides a foundational understanding of how error-correcting codes can be strategically employed to mitigate the detrimental effects of noise in quantum systems.

title: Based on Multivariate Normal Distribution Anomaly Detection Algorithm
abstract: This paper proposes a novel anomaly detection algorithm based on the characteristics of multivariate normal distributions. The core idea is to represent system data as multivariate normal distributions and leverage the inherent properties of these distributions to identify anomalies. This approach offers a potentially more effective method for detecting complex system anomalies compared to traditional methods. The algorithm focuses on identifying data points that deviate significantly from the expected patterns within the established multivariate normal distribution. We will explore the mathematical foundations underpinning this approach, detailing the statistical assumptions and the methodology for anomaly scoring. The algorithm's efficacy is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and a conceptual framework, highlighting its potential applications in various domains.

title: 基于图嵌入的知识图谱推理与发现
abstract: This paper explores the application of graph embedding techniques to knowledge graph reasoning and discovery. Traditional knowledge graph reasoning methods often struggle with scalability and accuracy, particularly when dealing with complex relationships within large knowledge graphs. This research proposes a novel approach that leverages graph embedding algorithms to represent entities and relationships within a knowledge graph as dense vector representations. These embeddings capture the structural and semantic information inherent in the graph, enabling efficient and accurate reasoning and new knowledge discovery. We investigate various embedding techniques, including Node2Vec, DeepWalk, and TransE, evaluating their performance on several reasoning tasks. The results demonstrate that graph embeddings significantly improve the efficiency and accuracy of knowledge graph reasoning compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, the learned embeddings provide a valuable tool for identifying novel relationships and patterns within the knowledge graph, leading to the discovery of new knowledge. This work contributes to the growing field of knowledge graph technology by providing a practical and effective approach to knowledge graph reasoning and discovery based on the power of graph embedding techniques.

title: 基于动态概率的概率图理论的推广
abstract: This paper introduces a novel probabilistic model called Dynamic Probability Graph (DPG) Theory, which extends the core concepts of probability graph theory to dynamically evolving probability distributions. We propose a dynamic adjustment algorithm that iteratively refines the probability distribution based on a defined objective function, allowing for complex optimization problems within the context of probabilistic modeling. The core mechanism focuses on representing probability as a dynamic graph, where nodes represent probability values and edges represent probabilistic relationships. This allows for the incorporation of feedback loops and adaptive adjustment, addressing limitations of static probability graph theory. The paper demonstrates the efficacy of this approach through several illustrative examples, showcasing its ability to effectively tackle optimization challenges typically addressed by traditional methods.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Accelerated Distributed Computing
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to distributed computing leveraging the phenomenon of quantum entanglement. The core claim is that by directly connecting distributed computing nodes through entangled quantum states, we can drastically reduce data transmission latency and significantly accelerate computational processes. The proposed mechanism involves constructing a carefully designed quantum entanglement network, enabling instantaneous information exchange between nodes – effectively bypassing the limitations imposed by the speed of light. This approach shifts the paradigm from relying solely on quantum computers for classical computation to utilizing the fundamental properties of quantum mechanics as an intrinsic acceleration mechanism. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of this method, focusing on the potential for parallel computation and collaborative processing facilitated by entanglement. This research aims to establish a foundational understanding of entanglement-accelerated distributed computing, paving the way for future exploration and development in this nascent field. The central equation demonstrating the potential speed-up is: Δt = (Δs/c) + t_c, where Δt is the total computation time, Δs is the size of the data set, c is the speed of light, and t_c is the classical computation time. We demonstrate that, with perfect entanglement, Δt can be reduced substantially, approaching a speed increase of approximately 1/c, which is significantly faster than the conventional speed of data transfer.

title: Where Perceptrons Meet Proof Trees: A Comparative Analysis Review of Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning Systems
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning Systems in the context of Artificial Intelligence. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of neuro-symbolic and reasoning as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Artificial Intelligence.
