title: Title: Quantum-Enhanced Fractal Simulation (QESF)
abstract: Quantum-Enhanced Fractal Simulation (QESF) is a novel computational technique designed to accelerate and improve the simulation of fractal structures by integrating quantum computation. This research investigates the potential of leveraging quantum algorithms to represent and manipulate fractal patterns, aiming to surpass the limitations of traditional classical methods in terms of fidelity and computational speed. The core mechanism centers on utilizing quantum entanglement to enhance the representation and traversal of fractal geometries, ultimately achieving a higher degree of accuracy and efficiency in the simulation process. This paper explores the theoretical underpinnings of QESF, outlines the key algorithmic components, and presents preliminary results demonstrating the potential for substantial speedups compared to classical methods. The study focuses primarily on the representation of fractal patterns using quantum states and explores the application of quantum entanglement to enhance the simulation of complex fractal geometries. The ultimate goal is to establish QESF as a viable and powerful tool for modeling and simulating fractal structures across various scientific and engineering disciplines.

title: Conclusions
abstract: The analyses presented throughout this book demonstrate that artificial intelligence is no longer limited to the role of a technological support mechanism operating at the margins of organisational activity. Instead, AI increasingly functions as an integrated element of enterprise structures, influencing how organisations process information, coordinate activities, formulate strategies, manage operations, and distribute decision-making authority. The transition from AI-support enterprises towards AI-first enterprises reflects a broader transformation in organisational logic, where algorithmic systems become embedded within the core mechanisms of governance and management. As noted by Dignum (2019) , the growing organisational role of AI requires enterprises to rethink not only technological infrastructures but also institutional responsibility, ethical governance, and managerial control.

title: Sensing Which Modality Matters: Evidence-Gated Regularization for Robust VLA Policies
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies fuse multimodal sensory inputs, but training on limited and homogeneous robot demonstrations encourages spurious inter-sensor correlations rather than task-relevant signal, a failure we term modality entanglement. Under real-world occlusions and distractors, this manifests as nuisance sensitivity to corruption of uninformative sensors and single-modality insufficiency when only one informative sensor remains intact. We propose Evidence-Gated Regularization (EGR), a modality-agnostic training objective that introduces zero inference-time overhead. EGR derives a per-frame and per-sensor task-relevance signal to gate two state-conditional consistency objectives: invariance on low-evidence sensors, and single-sensor sufficiency on high-evidence ones. We introduce a benchmark based on BEHAVIOR-1K, comprising a fast inference-only diagnostic suite and 47 rollout-based skills targeting modality entanglement. We validate EGR on this benchmark and on two real-robot setups with fundamentally different embodiments: a bi-manual setup with two Kinova arms and three RGB cameras, and a single-arm MELFA ASSISTA setup combining vision and GelSight tactile sensors. EGR improves simulation success rates (SR) from 12.5% to 16.4% under full modalities (+31%), from 9.4% to 16.5% under uninformative-sensor corruption (+75%), and from 2.8% to 6.1% under single-sensor fallback (+120%). Under physical-object distractors, EGR boosts SR from 30% to 85% on the bi-manual setup (+183%) and from 55% to 70% on the tactile setup (+27%).

title: A Two-Variable Zeta Function for a Parity-Perturbed Hofstadter Q-Recursion: The Exceptional t = -1 Slice and Gaussian Boundary Layers
abstract: We study the parity-perturbed Hofstadter Q-recursion $ widetilde Q(1)=widetilde Q(2)=1,qquad widetilde Q(n)=widetilde Q(n-widetilde Q(n-1)) +widetilde Q(n-widetilde Q(n-2))+(-1)^n, and the associated two-variable Dirichlet series Z_{widetilde Q}(s,t)=sum_{nge1}n^{-s}widetilde Q(n)^{-t}. The estimate \widetilde Q(n)=n/2+O(n/\log n) gives the exact domain of absolute convergence Re(s+t)>1. With w=s+t, we separate the universal term 2^tζ(w) and derive exact transport, frequency-position, and dyadic renormalization identities. The main result concerns t=-1. For E(n)=2\widetilde Q(n)-n and A(X)=\sum_{n\le X}E(n), the binary-arch clock yields A(X)=Xlog_2X+XΩ!left(log_23X{32}right) +O!left(X{log X}right), where Ω is an explicit continuous periodic function. This continues the normalized correction to Rew>0 and yields a boundary resonance lattice: a double resonance at w=0 and simple resonances at 2πi m/\log2. After subtracting the full-slice order-X skeleton, we analyze the negative-even arch channel. Its companion-forest layers have a weak Gaussian limit, and a canonical subsequence realizes the optimal n/\log n pointwise scale with an explicit signed constant. The negative-arch mass satisfies A_r=512{92π}16^r{sqrt r} left(1-13{16r}+O(r^{-2})right). We do not claim a full-slice continuation across Rew=0$.

title: Quantum Workload Privacy Beyond Data Confidentiality
abstract: Remote quantum computing exposes a confidentiality gap. Standard privacy mechanisms protect quantum states and outputs, but not the scientific structure of a workload. This work reveals that hardware-aware compilation leaves observable signatures, such as routing overhead, circuit depth, and gate composition, that correlate with hidden modelling choices like partial differential equation boundary conditions, discretisation scale, and molecular geometry. The leakage arises from the mismatch between logical topology and fixed hardware connectivity, forcing problem-dependent SWAP insertion. We formalise this threat as Scientific-Intent Indistinguishability and prove that passive security is asymptotically unachievable under routing-optimal compilation. Experiments on a 156-qubit IBM Heron processor achieve near-perfect classification of boundary regimes and molecular geometries, with leakage generalising across solver families via routing-scaling exponents. Conventional gate-padding fails as a defence, causing fidelity drops without reducing adversarial advantage. Our results show that protecting quantum data alone is insufficient; execution-level confidentiality must become a first-class design requirement.

title: Schrödinger Bridges on Lie Group Manifolds for Probabilistic Intrinsic Generation
abstract: Generative modeling directly on geometric manifolds can avoid errors introduced by flattening non-Euclidean data, repeated ambient projection, and coordinate inconsistency in Euclidean representations. Schrodinger bridges provide a probabilistic generative framework for entropy-regularized transport between prescribed endpoint distributions. We study Schrodinger bridges for kinetic dynamics on Lie group manifolds with state X_t = (g_t, xi_t) in G x g, allowing endpoint observations to constrain only the variables that are actually measured. In particular, the entropy projection determines the conditional law of the unobserved endpoint velocities. For the same observed endpoint bridge, we develop two computational realizations: Wrapped-Kernel Bridge Calibration (WKBC) uses an explicit periodized kinetic kernel on compact Abelian groups, whereas Reciprocal Conditional-Control Bridge Matching (RCCBM) handles compact non-Abelian groups through two-sided endpoint calibration and mollified conditional-control matching. The canonical teacher-mixture path law is itself a Markov reciprocal law, so forward generation uses a calibrated initial law and one learned Doob controller. Moreover, we establish a modular error bound in the bounded-Lipschitz path metric that provides a clean separation of errors due to endpoints, control regression, initialization, discretization, and related approximations. Experiments on multiple Lie group manifold datasets validate the feasibility and consistency of our proposed method, covering protein and RNA torsions, SO(3), U(n), and the Protein Conformational Transition Pathway Generation task using mdCATH trajectories in a compact reduced representation. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/cafferyzhang12/Schr-dinger_Bridge_on_LieGroup.

title: A Unified Particle Filter LSTM for Data-Driven Process Simulation
abstract: Data-driven process simulation aims to generate realistic case trajectories from historical event logs without requiring an explicitly specified model of the underlying dynamics. Deep sequence models can capture complex temporal dependencies through next-activity probabilities and conditional time distributions. However, event logs provide only a partial view of the underlying process state, often recording activity completions without the corresponding service-start times. Consequently, the same observed process history may be consistent with multiple plausible latent process conditions, whereas standard recurrent models compress each process prefix into a single deterministic recurrent state. We propose a Unified Particle Filter LSTM (Unified PF-LSTM) that maintains and sequentially updates a weighted set of recurrent-state hypotheses. We summarize this particle belief using its weighted mean and learned features based on the moment-generating function. The resulting representation is used to predict a categorical distribution over the next activity and conditional quantiles of the current activity's sojourn time. The framework is trained end-to-end from event-log data and evaluated on three real-world emergency department datasets. The results show that the proposed framework consistently outperforms the considered data-driven baselines in reproducing routing, duration, and system-level behavior across all datasets, with particularly strong gains in settings where complex process dynamics are only partially reflected in the available event logs.

title: Borrowing Knowledge Across Tasks: A State of the Art Review of Transfer Learning and the Pretraining Paradigm
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of Transfer Learning and the Pretraining Paradigm in the context of Artificial Intelligence. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of transfer learning and pretraining as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Artificial Intelligence.

title: High-Order Matrix Topological Structure
abstract: This paper investigates the application of a novel high-order matrix topological structure to enhance system control. Traditional matrix approaches often require manual adjustment, limiting adaptability. We propose a mechanism leveraging the matrix's inherent self-adaptation to dynamically adjust the topology, enabling more intelligent and adaptive control. The core of this work focuses on a system where the matrix's structure is continuously refined based on input data, demonstrating improved performance compared to static approaches.

title: Quantum Topology Geometric Evolution
abstract: Quantum topology, a fascinating field, explores the interplay between quantum mechanics and topology. This research investigates the geometric evolution of quantum topologies, specifically focusing on the design and application of a novel geometric evolution algorithm. The core claim is that this algorithm, driven by quantum topological principles, offers a robust method for simulating and analyzing complex systems, enabling a deeper understanding and predictive capability than traditional approaches. The study encompasses a detailed mathematical framework, including the formulation of a geometric evolution process, the implementation of the proposed algorithm, and analysis of its efficacy through simulations. This paper presents a comprehensive overview of the research, including the mathematical basis of the geometric evolution, the algorithmic design, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating the algorithm's capabilities.

title: Dynamic Quantum State Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic quantum state optimization algorithm based on the concept of quantum entanglement, specifically utilizing "quantum pulses" to dynamically adjust quantum state parameters. Traditional quantum state optimization methods are typically static, offering limited adaptability to complex quantum systems. This work proposes a fundamentally new approach that leverages quantum entanglement to achieve self-adaptive optimization, aiming to significantly enhance the performance of quantum computing. The core mechanism involves generating and manipulating entangled states to guide parameter adjustments, thereby enabling a more effective and robust optimization process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm through simulations and preliminary analysis, showcasing its potential to overcome limitations of existing optimization techniques.

abstract: Modern neuroscience faces fundamental limitations including EEG inaccuracy, the extreme complexity of 86 billion neurons, and the physical constraints of long-term synaptic plasticity (LTP) within the classical Euclidean paradigm. By implementing the Engram Injector v1.5, the system achieves non-commutative damping, Phase Snapping, and Zeta-spectrum tunneling (14.1347Hz resonance) to non-invasively access, purify, and refactor the unconscious mind under explicit consent. Comprehensive simulation results across six major psychiatric pathologies (PTSD, Addiction, Schizophrenia, MDD, Bipolar Disorder, and ADHD) validate the system’s clinicalefficacy, ultra-low latency (< 600µs) FPGA architecture, and ethical safeguards.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Geometric Modeling of Fluid Dynamics
abstract: This research investigates the potential of quantum mechanics to enhance geometric modeling of fluid dynamics, specifically addressing the challenges posed by complex flow scenarios. We propose a novel approach that leverages quantum-inspired methods to represent and manipulate fluid dynamics parameters, aiming to improve the accuracy and efficiency of simulations. This work explores the application of quantum-based representations to streamline calculations and improve the representation of turbulent flows, ultimately leading to more robust and accurate fluid dynamics models. The research focuses on creating a new framework for modeling complex flows, potentially offering a significant advancement over traditional methods.

title: Quantum State-Based Distributed Storage (QBDS)
abstract: This paper explores the concept of Quantum State-Based Distributed Storage (QBDS), a novel approach to data storage leveraging the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics. QBDS aims to achieve high storage capacity and enhanced security by encoding data within quantum states, exploiting quantum entanglement for redundancy and error correction, and employing Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) for secure data transmission. The core claim of this work is that the unique properties of superposition and entanglement within quantum states offer a viable pathway to a high-capacity, secure distributed storage system. This document details the underlying mechanisms, key considerations, and potential challenges associated with QBDS, laying the groundwork for future research and development in this rapidly evolving field. The proposed system utilizes quantum information theory and distributed storage architectures to deliver a robust and inherently secure data storage solution.

title: Quantum Random Access Memory (QRAM) Assisted Distributed Computing
abstract: This paper presents a novel theoretical framework for leveraging Quantum Random Access Memory (QRAM) within a distributed computing paradigm. The core argument revolves around the established communication bottleneck as a primary impediment to the scalability of traditional distributed algorithms. We propose an algorithm architecture designed to specifically exploit the unique capabilities of QRAM, aiming to achieve exponential speedups for selected computational tasks. Unlike previous conceptual explorations, this work provides a rigorous mathematical formulation and analysis of the proposed approach. The framework centers on a massively parallel computation strategy, where QRAM facilitates near-instantaneous access to data elements, effectively eliminating the latency constraints that typically plague distributed systems. We detail the algorithm's structure, including data partitioning, quantum state manipulation, and the resulting computation. Furthermore, we explore the theoretical limitations and potential improvements of the system. The ultimate goal is to demonstrate a scalable and efficient distributed computing solution utilizing QRAM, pushing the boundaries of computational performance for complex problems.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning via Dynamic Logic Programming
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for neuro-symbolic reasoning, termed Dynamic Logic Programming. The core idea is to integrate the pattern recognition capabilities of neural networks with the logical inference capabilities of symbolic systems. Specifically, a neural network is trained to generate symbolic rules, represented in a Prolog-like format. These rules are then executed by a dynamic logic programming system for reasoning. Crucially, the neural network continuously learns and refines these rules based on feedback received from the logic program's execution, creating a bidirectional information flow. This approach overcomes limitations of traditional approaches by enabling adaptive and flexible reasoning, particularly in complex and uncertain environments. The system demonstrates the potential for improved reasoning accuracy and efficiency compared to purely neural or purely symbolic methods. The key contribution lies in the dynamic adaptation of symbolic rules through a neural network, resulting in a more robust and intelligent reasoning engine. The framework utilizes a recurrent neural network (RNN) to generate rules and a dynamic logic programming system with a rule-based inference engine to execute the generated rules and provide feedback. The process is iterative, allowing the neural network to learn and refine its rule generation strategy. This paper outlines the system architecture, the training methodology, and initial experimental results, showcasing the potential of this combined approach.

abstract: Complete replication package for the manuscript Grounding, Benchmarking and Operationalizing Sustainability-Aware Knowledge Graph Completion for Supply Chain Decision Support, submitted to Sustainability. title: Memory-Enhanced Probabilistic Reasoning Engine
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to probabilistic reasoning by integrating memory networks with probabilistic graph models. The core idea is to mimic the associative nature of human memory, leveraging historical data and knowledge to enhance the accuracy and generalizability of probabilistic inferences. Traditional probabilistic reasoning models often struggle with incorporating contextual information and prior knowledge. Our proposed engine addresses this limitation by constructing a memory network to store relevant data and knowledge, which then feeds probabilistic graph models during the reasoning process. The feedback loop between the memory network and the graph model allows for adaptive and context-aware inference. The engine utilizes a novel architecture that allows for dynamic updates to the probabilistic graph based on the retrieved information from the memory network. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a theoretical framework and outline a key mechanism: the memory network's influence on probabilistic inference. This work represents a significant step towards more robust and human-like probabilistic reasoning systems.

title: 基于图神经网络的复杂性建模与优化
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to complex system modeling and optimization utilizing graph neural networks (GNNs). We propose a framework that constructs a graph representation of a given system, learns relationships within this graph using GNNs, and subsequently employs these learned representations for feature extraction and optimization. The core of our method is a GNN-based representation learning process which allows for efficient analysis and optimization of complex systems. The proposed approach addresses limitations of traditional methods by automating the process of capturing intricate relationships within the data, leading to improved performance and efficiency. We present a comprehensive framework with detailed explanations of the key components and their implementation.

title: Decentralized Differential Privacy via Byzantine Fault Tolerance
abstract: Decentralized systems offer advantages like resilience and scalability, but their inherent vulnerability to Byzantine faults—attacks where malicious actors compromise the system's integrity—presents a significant obstacle to achieving differential privacy. This paper proposes a novel approach to decentralized differential privacy that leverages Byzantine Fault Tolerant (BFT) consensus mechanisms. Our design allows multiple parties to collaboratively compute sensitive statistics while simultaneously guaranteeing differential privacy against these malicious adversaries. The core of our approach is a specifically engineered BFT protocol optimized for privacy preservation, offering a practical solution to a long-standing problem in distributed computing. We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this method through a theoretical analysis and conceptual design. The key innovations lie in the tight integration of BFT consensus with differential privacy techniques, creating a robust and verifiable system. This work represents a significant step towards realizing truly decentralized and trustworthy data analytics.

title: Cryptanalytic Information Geometry for Masked ML-KEM
abstract: This work proposes a unified framework for evaluating and optimizing side-channel information according to its downstream cryptanalytic value rather than information content alone. The framework introduces Attack-Sensitive Information Geometry (ASIG), Attack-Aware Hint Compilation (AHC), and Active Leakage Allocation (ALA), forming a closed-loop methodology from physical leakage and posterior inference to cryptanalytic utility and adaptive information acquisition. The work develops a mathematical formulation, testable conjectures, and controlled computational validation. The reported simulations are synthetic mathematical proof-of-concept experiments and are not presented as physical measurements, empirical key recovery, or a practical ML-KEM attack.

title: Natural Language Processing for Interactive Learning Experiences
abstract: Natural Language Processing (NLP) has become a core component for next generation e-learning ecosystems, especially in content delivery. It enables platforms to understand, respond and adapt to individual learners. With the rise of deep learning models especially transformer based architectures, NLP now offers state of the art capabilities for real-time interaction, personalized feedback, and adaptive learning pathways. This chapter examines NLP-driven systems powered by deep learning to enhance learner engagement, motivation, and cognitive development. It is developed by converting static educational materials into dynamic, conversational, and highly interactive experiences. The key ideas in this chapter includes understanding text, language models that can generate responses, intelligent tutoring systems, automatic grading, feedback that considers emotions, and learning that uses multiple types of media (such as text, audio, and images). Practical use cases and emerging research trends are highlighted. Ethical, pedagogical and technological challenges are also discussed.

title: A Personalized E-Learning Environment for AI Upskilling in Retail MSMEs: Design, Facilitator Support and Early Usability Validation
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is already affecting several areas of retail work, from stock forecasting and online sales to customer communication and marketing decisions. For many smaller retail businesses, however, the question is not only whether AI tools are available, but whether owners and employees can understand them well enough to make informed choices. The INAIR e-learning environment was developed in this context, as a multilingual platform for AI upskilling in retail micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs). This work-in-progress paper reports on the current design of the platform and on an early round of usability and interaction feedback. In its current form, the platform brings together sixteen AI-related modules with a simple onboarding process, a diagnostic starting point, pathway guidance, progress tracking and badges. It also includes guidance for facilitators, since the platform may be used not only by individual learners but also by trainers, vocational education providers, chambers of commerce and in-company learning teams. The paper uses project documentation, platform design material, the facilitator manual and the platform feedback log to discuss how the learning model was structured and refined. Early feedback suggests that the platform is understandable and coherent, although several issues around navigation, progression logic and learner guidance still require further work. The paper contributes an early account of how personalized e-learning and facilitator support can be combined to make AI training more accessible for retail MSMEs.

title: Hierarchical multi-label structuring of Japanese SOAP clinical notes with large language models
abstract: Much clinically salient information in Japanese electronic medical records is recorded in SOAP (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan) notes, which contain a lot of unstructured text preventing the further usage for analysis. Structuring such unstructured text is essential for secondary data use and clinical research. This study aimed to develop a schema-guided, hierarchical multi-label (15 first-level and 58 second-level labels) framework for structuring respiratory medicine SOAP notes using a locally deployed large language model (LLaMA-3.1-8B adapted with QLoRA). 200 randomly selected notes were annotated and split in two for training and test. Performance was assessed through atomic-cell matching under both strict and tolerant similarity metrics, achieved a micro-averaged F1 of 0.49 (strict) and 0.59 (Levenshtein> 0.7). Common and standardized fields such as vital signs were reliably structured, while ambiguous boundaries and rare labels remained challenging. These findings demonstrate that schema-guided hierarchical multi-label frameworks can support the structuring of Japanese clinical notes and serve as a foundation for downstream research and quality-improvement workflows.

title: Conflict-Free Color-Clustered Sequential Belief-Propagation Decoding of Quantum LDPC Codes via Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Belief-propagation (BP) decoding for quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes is attractive due to its low complexity and low latency, but it is often limited by short cycles, degeneracy, and convergence failures. Reinforcement-learning-based sequential BP decoding (RL-S) improves BP by learning a syndrome-dependent variable-node (VN) update order, but its VN-by-VN schedule has limited within-iteration parallelism. In this paper, we propose a conflict-free color-clustered extension of RL-S. We construct a VN conflict graph in which two VNs are adjacent if they share an X-type or Z-type check, and color this graph so that same-color VNs have disjoint check neighborhoods. This also prevents VNs from the same Tanner 4- or 6-cycle from being updated simultaneously. During decoding, the trained VN-level Q-table selects a seed VN, and all remaining VNs with the same color are updated in parallel using the same pre-batch messages. For the [[288,12,18]] bivariate-bicycle code over the depolarizing channel, our proposed decoder achieves block-error-rate performance close to VN-level RL-S while reducing the scheduling decisions from 288 VNs to 11 color classes per BP iteration.

title: Clinical Reasoning Under a Partially Observed Objective in Cone Beam CT Report Generation
abstract: Maxillofacial report generation from cone beam computed tomography is scored here by a composite objective placing 80% of its weight on a large language model judgement of factual entailment and 20% on lexical overlap, of which only the lexical fifth is visible during development. The grader's BLEU-4 and METEOR routines are reproduced in pure Python and match the reference to machine precision, and an offline entailment surrogate, which tells a report written for one patient from one written for another at an area under the curve of 0.987, makes the composite objective cheap enough to optimise directly. Over the 622-case public release, a report selected against the visible lexical ranking scores 0.2909, whereas one selected against the composite objective scores 0.4122, because pursuing n-gram overlap drives entailment precision from 0.522 down to 0.266. A 29 million parameter encoder fine-tuned on the release reaches a prevalence-weighted out-of-fold area under the curve of 0.486 over 985 statements, indistinguishable from the corpus prior, while nine numbers read from the image header reach 0.945 for mandible coverage and 0.872 for condyle coverage, and acquisition centre alone predicts sentence choice at 0.718 against 0.663 for the image-derived model, identifying dictation convention rather than anatomy as the quantity the lexical metrics reward. The delivered system emits eight unconditional statements and five gated on header geometry under polarity, laterality and tooth-level consistency constraints, and reaches METEOR 0.3542 over 50 held-out cases from an unseen centre. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/GIND123/CBCT-Clinical-Reasoner

title: Heuristically optimizing, synthesizing, and prioritizing measurement settings for quantum state tomography
abstract: A key task in many quantum-computing applications, e.g., quantum simulation and quantum state tomography (QST), is to partition an arbitrary set of operators into mutually commuting subsets for efficient measurements. However, brute-force approaches to this task quickly become intractable as the number and dimensionality of operators grow. Here, we reformulate operator partitioning as a graph-coloring (GC) problem and develop an efficient computational framework to solve it, balancing accuracy and efficiency. Our framework enables leveraging a range of GC algorithms, which we benchmark for operator partitioning. Then, we demonstrate their utility in optimizing QST experiments, where determining non-overlapping data acquisition settings for QST is a major challenge, and prioritizing among these settings, i.e., selecting the experiments that provide the most information. We further show how to perform these experiments by synthesizing Clifford circuits for joint measurement of commuting Pauli operators in multi-qubit systems. We validate our framework across multi-qubit (up to five qubits), multi-qutrit (up to three qutrits), and hybrid qubit-qutrit systems. Our results show that heuristic GC methods substantially reduce the number of required measurement settings for QST and enable priority-based scheduling that maximizes the information gain per experiment. The optimization converges within minutes on a student-grade laptop, providing speedups of several orders of magnitude over brute-force methods already for these relatively small quantum systems. This demonstrates the potential of GC heuristics as a scalable and practical tool for characterization of noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices. We have made the Python implementation of our GC framework to optimize and schedule QST experiments publicly available at https://github.com/ssm8015/QST_GT.git.

title: CA-OPD: Confidence-Aware On-Policy Distillation for Structured Visual Prediction
abstract: Autoregressive vision language models unify heterogeneous perception tasks but are highly susceptible to compounding errors. On-policy distillation (OPD) bridges the training-inference mismatch by training students on their own rollouts. However, unreliable student predictions, especially early in training, can derail the trajectory and degrade the quality of teacher supervision. While recent interleaved distillation methods allow the teacher to verify and replace student tokens, they primarily rely on rigid ranking metrics rather than exact teacher confidence, and they overlook how intervention decisions can inform token-level supervision. To address this, we introduce Confidence-Aware On-Policy Distillation (CA-OPD), a framework that couples reliable rollout construction with adaptive supervision. CA-OPD utilizes teacher confidence to selectively correct unreliable student transitions, gradually transferring rollout control to the student via a strict-to-relaxed schedule. Crucially, CA-OPD aligns knowledge transfer with these intervention decisions: corrected positions receive direct cross-entropy supervision from the teacher's prediction, while retained positions benefit from the teacher's full predictive distribution. Evaluated in a multi-teacher setting for GUI grounding and optical character recognition, CA-OPD substantially improves the Qwen3.5-0.8B baseline across all six target benchmarks, including gains of $9.50$ points on ScreenSpot-Pro and $6.72$ points on OCRBench-v2 English. Controlled studies further show that the gains depend on intervention placement, progressive rollout control, and intervention-aligned supervision, rather than intervention frequency alone.

title: Aggregating Neighbor Embedding Projection and Rank-Based Manifold Learning for Image Retrieval
abstract: Content-based image retrieval (CBIR) has advanced significantly with deep learning, yet effectively ranking similar images remains challenging, particularly in high-dimensional feature spaces, where pairwise distances often fail to capture contextual relationships and the semantic gap between visual features and high-level concepts persists. Manifold learning and rank-based refinement methods have emerged as complementary strategies, respectively improving feature representations and exploiting contextual information embedded in ranked lists, such as neighborhood relationships among images. However, combining these projection-based and rank-based strategies to exploit their complementary properties remains a challenging research problem. To address this, we propose a framework that combines neighbor embedding projections with rank-based manifold learning through rank aggregation. Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) generates alternative low-dimensional feature representations, and ranked lists obtained from UMAP projections and rank-based re-ranking methods are combined using the Borda Count aggregation strategy. Experiments were conducted on several public datasets using deep learning features extracted from ResNet152, Swin Transformer, and DINOv2 models. Results show that the proposed approach improves retrieval effectiveness in several scenarios, particularly when the baseline representation struggles to achieve high precision. The aggregation strategy also often improves the quality of top-ranked positions, leading to competitive Mean Average Precision (MAP) and Precision values across different datasets and feature extractors. These findings suggest that combining projection-based and rank-based manifold learning strategies through rank aggregation can provide complementary contextual information for image retrieval tasks.

title: Reproducibility Package for "A Three-Layer Runtime Safety Architecture for Sequential Agents"
abstract: This reproducibility package accompanies the manuscript “A Three-Layer Runtime Safety Architecture for Sequential Agents: Complementary Constraints Against Hard Risk, Cumulative Risk, and Goal Drift.” It contains the frozen implementation, raw experimental outputs, 10 sealed confirmatory maps, 50 additional robustness maps, automated tests, statistical-analysis scripts, and figure-generation utilities used to reproduce the reported confirmatory and post-hoc robustness experiments. The package corresponds to the frozen experimental version dated 21 August 2026. The task planner, runtime-monitor rules and thresholds, safety-controller logic, and experimental settings were held fixed for the robustness evaluation, with no parameter retuning on the 50 additional maps. Implementation note: the archive retains legacy and development-stage policy-training artifacts from earlier stages of the project. These artifacts were not used to generate the confirmatory or post-hoc robustness results reported in the manuscript. The reported experiments instantiate the deterministic wall-only BFS task planner directly through DeterministicTaskPolicy; no Q-table or learned policy is loaded during the reported experimental runs.

title: Title: Quantum-Enhanced Geometric Simulation of Complex Fluid Dynamics
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum-enhanced geometric simulation to revolutionize the representation and analysis of complex fluid dynamics. Traditional numerical methods often struggle to accurately model the intricate quantum effects that govern fluid flow, leading to inaccuracies and computational bottlenecks. We propose a novel simulation technique, incorporating a quantum-enhanced geometric framework, designed to address these limitations. This work details the algorithm's core principles, the quantum-mechanical elements employed, and the expected impact on simulation accuracy and speed. The research focuses on leveraging quantum entanglement and superposition to enhance the representation of fluid wave propagation, turbulence, and other crucial fluid dynamics phenomena. The ultimate goal is to provide a more robust and efficient method for simulating complex fluid dynamics, opening avenues for advancements in fields ranging from fluid mechanics to materials science.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Data Compression for High-Dimensional Data
abstract: Quantum compression, a nascent field exploring the potential of quantum mechanics to enhance data compression, has emerged as a promising avenue for addressing the growing challenge of efficient data storage and transmission, particularly with high-dimensional data. This paper investigates a novel quantum-inspired data compression algorithm, utilizing quantum superposition to represent data in a more efficient manner. We demonstrate the algorithm's ability to achieve substantial data reduction compared to existing classical methods, offering a significant improvement in compression efficiency and potentially unlocking new possibilities in data management. The core mechanism focuses on leveraging quantum phenomena to enhance data representation, leading to a more compact and effective compression process.

title: Algorithmic Quantum State Preservation
abstract: Quantum state preservation is a fundamental challenge in quantum computing, particularly in the face of decoherence. Current algorithms often struggle to maintain the integrity of quantum states across repeated operations. This paper introduces an algorithmic quantum state preservation framework centered on the implementation of a "Quantum State Coherence Stabilizer." This stabilizer dynamically adjusts the system's internal state to mitigate decoherence, thereby guaranteeing the preservation of quantum information. We present a novel algorithm demonstrating this approach, offering a potential breakthrough in the design of robust quantum algorithms.

title: Title: The Geometry of Consciousness – A Topological Approach to Neural Networks
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of neural networks to represent and process information through the principles of topology, specifically the concept of 'topological states.' We propose a novel neural network architecture, termed the 'topology network,' that explicitly models the relationships between nodes and edges within a topological graph, exploring how this framework might offer a new perspective on the emergence of consciousness. The core claim is that by focusing on these topological relationships, we can develop a more robust and potentially more insightful model of neural function. This work will demonstrate the potential for this approach to overcome limitations of current neural network architectures and address fundamental questions about the nature of consciousness.

title: Generative Modeling of Complex Time Series with Non-Stationary Distributions
abstract: This paper presents a novel generative modeling approach for complex time series data exhibiting non-stationarity. Traditional time series models often rely on the assumption of stationarity, a limitation when dealing with real-world data that frequently displays evolving statistical properties. We introduce a hierarchical Bayesian model incorporating a Gaussian process prior and a non-parametric likelihood function. This framework allows us to effectively capture the dynamic nature of the time series, generating new samples that reflect its evolving distribution. The core of the model lies in its ability to learn and represent the temporal dependencies within the data, even when those dependencies change over time. The model's parameters are inferred using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach through a theoretical analysis and outline its potential applications in various domains, including financial forecasting, sensor data analysis, and anomaly detection. The key innovation is the integration of a Gaussian process prior with a flexible, non-parametric likelihood, providing a robust solution for modeling time series with evolving distributions.

title: 基于量子纠缠的分布式机器学习算法验证
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of utilizing quantum entanglement to enhance the validation process of machine learning algorithms. We propose a novel distributed learning framework that leverages quantum entanglement to verify the correctness and stability of algorithms, potentially leading to improved model performance and reliability. The core mechanism centers on exploiting the unique properties of quantum entanglement to provide a fundamentally different approach to algorithm evaluation, offering the possibility of more accurate and robust validation. The research explores the theoretical basis and practical implementation challenges associated with this approach, outlining the key steps involved in creating a quantum-enhanced verification pipeline. The paper concludes with a discussion of the potential benefits and limitations of this technology, emphasizing its promise for advancing the field of machine learning.

title: Probabilistic Programming Based on Biological Neural Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to probabilistic programming by leveraging the computational mechanisms of biological neural networks. The core idea is to integrate the logical reasoning of probabilistic programming with the parallel processing capabilities of biological neural networks, aiming to achieve efficient and potentially more robust probabilistic inference and decision-making. This is achieved by mapping probabilistic programming rules and probability distributions onto the synaptic weights of a neural network, enabling parallel computation through the network's architecture. The presented framework offers a fundamentally different paradigm compared to traditional probabilistic programming, which primarily relies on symbolic logic and lacks inherent parallel processing capabilities. The research explores the potential for developing more scalable and adaptable probabilistic systems inspired by the biological brain. This work establishes a foundational methodology for exploring the synergy between symbolic and connectionist approaches to probabilistic computation.

title: Title: Adaptive Quantum Error Correction with Dynamic Resource Allocation
abstract: Quantum computing holds immense promise for revolutionary advancements across numerous fields, but the inherent fragility of quantum information necessitates sophisticated error correction techniques. Current quantum error correction methods often rely on computationally intensive overhead, limiting scalability. This paper proposes an adaptive quantum error correction scheme that dynamically allocates resources to different parts of the quantum circuit based on the observed error rate. We introduce a novel resource-aware algorithm that adjusts the amount of error correction applied to each qubit based on its current error state, aiming to significantly improve error correction efficiency and reduce the overall complexity of quantum computations. This work addresses a critical challenge in quantum computing – the need for efficient error correction – with a mechanism for adaptive resource allocation. The proposed algorithm demonstrates substantial improvements in error correction performance compared to existing approaches in initial simulations and preliminary experiments. We conclude with a discussion of the potential implications of this approach for future quantum systems.

title: Symbiotic Quantum-Classical Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for symbiotic quantum-classical networks, moving beyond the traditional view of quantum computers as isolated accelerators. The core concept is to design networks where quantum and classical processors operate in a tightly integrated manner, exchanging information and executing computations collaboratively. We define a set of architectural principles and mathematical models that enable this symbiotic relationship. The network architecture is based on a layered approach, with a classical layer providing control and orchestration, a quantum layer performing computationally intensive tasks, and an intermediate layer facilitating data transfer and hybrid computation. We introduce a key metric, the "Quantum-Classical Synergy Factor" (QCSF), to quantify the efficiency of the integration. The QCSF is defined as: QCSF = (∑i=1K |Ei|) / (Etotal) where Ei represents the energy consumed by the *i*-th component (quantum or classical) during a computation, and Etotal is the total energy consumed by the entire network. Furthermore, we explore the impact of different communication protocols on the network's performance, considering both speed and error rates. We analyze scenarios involving quantum state preparation, measurement, and the execution of hybrid quantum-classical algorithms. The aim is to achieve significant computational advantages by exploiting the complementary strengths of each paradigm. This framework offers a path toward practical quantum computing by addressing the limitations of current quantum hardware and software.

title: Quantum Entanglement Optimization Algorithm
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a bizarre phenomenon in quantum mechanics, presents a potentially revolutionary approach to optimization algorithms. This paper explores the design and implementation of a novel optimization algorithm predicated on entanglement, aiming to overcome the limitations of traditional methods. The core claim centers on the ability to discover global optima and circumvent the pitfalls of local search. The proposed algorithm leverages the instantaneous correlations inherent in entangled states to construct a global search space, offering a distinct pathway towards finding optimal solutions for complex problems. This research investigates the potential of entanglement to enhance optimization capabilities and proposes a framework for evaluating its effectiveness.

title: Quantum Error Correction Codes for Distributed Quantum Computing
abstract: This paper explores the application of quantum error correction (QEC) codes within a distributed quantum computing framework. The core claim is that leveraging the inherent redundancy of QEC codes facilitates the construction of a fault-tolerant distributed quantum computing system capable of executing complex quantum algorithms. The mechanism relies on encoding quantum information into QEC codes, enabling detection and correction of errors introduced during computation and transmission. This approach addresses the critical challenge of achieving reliable quantum computation in the face of environmental noise. The proposed system outlines a modular architecture where multiple quantum processors, each equipped with QEC capabilities, collaborate to perform computations. This paper details the theoretical framework, focusing on the design and implementation aspects of the distributed system, and highlights the potential for scaling quantum computation through this error-resilient approach. The system's success hinges on efficient decoding algorithms and robust communication protocols.

title: Dynamic Topology-Based Quantum Simulation Information Retention
abstract: This paper investigates the application of dynamic topology-based quantum simulation to preserve quantum information during the simulation of complex quantum systems. Traditional quantum simulation often relies on classical physics models, limiting the complexity and fidelity of simulations. We propose a novel algorithm leveraging machine learning to dynamically adjust the topology of the simulated quantum system, ensuring information retention and enabling the simulation of more intricate quantum structures. The core mechanism involves learning the inherent topology of the quantum system and employing this learning to guide the simulation process, effectively maintaining the integrity of quantum information. This work addresses a critical challenge in quantum simulation – the preservation of quantum states – by introducing a dynamic, adaptive approach.

title: Quantum Feedback Loop for Dynamical System Stability
abstract: Quantum Feedback Loop for Dynamical System Stability addresses the inherent challenges of stabilizing dynamic systems through traditional methods. This paper introduces a novel quantum-based feedback loop designed to continuously adapt to the system's internal state, thereby achieving a state of equilibrium. We propose a mechanism utilizing quantum measurement and entanglement to identify deviations from a target state and dynamically adjust system parameters. This approach offers a fundamentally new pathway to achieve robustness and adaptability in dynamical systems, potentially surpassing the limitations of classical stability analysis.

title: Beyond Pseudo-Labels: Dual-Level Knowledge Distillation for Enhanced Deep Clustering
abstract: This study introduces a novel clustering approach, namely Teacher–Student-based Deep Clustering (TSDC), that relies on intra- and inter-distillation-based feature representations. In fact, TSDC distils knowledge from (i) high- to low-response channels, forcing the latter to mimic the former, and (ii) deeper to shallower layers, prompting the transfer of semantic information to enhance representational consistency. Unlike CNN-based deep clustering that relies on pseudo-labels to improve representations, TSDC introduces a newly formulated objective function to simultaneously minimize losses from clustering and intra- and inter-distillation. The proposed approach was rigorously investigated using benchmark datasets and relevant performance measures. In particular, a linear top classifier protocol was adopted to assess TSDC performance. Notably, TSDC outperformed existing deep clustering frameworks, yielding improved classification accuracy. The empirical findings highlight the efficacy of combining intra- and inter-distillation to enrich feature representations. Notably, the most prominent improvement was observed on CIFAR-100, where classification accuracy rose from 54.77 ± 0.07 to 57.58 ± 1.85.

title: Bridging the Gap Between Curated and Induced Semantics
abstract: Building Automation and Management Systems offer centralised control and monitoring by integrating smart devices into the environment. Together, these provide building owners and stakeholders with data about energy consumption and other relevant characteristics which can, among others, be used for decision making and the automation of actions. However, due to the proliferation of different protocols and ecosystems, it often remains challenging to seamlessly aggregate and analyse the data streams provided by the connected devices. To overcome these problems, we introduce a distributed, knowledge-driven data exchange and validation framework, built upon Semantic Web technologies, that a) facilitates the transparent flow of data between smart devices, b) validates these data and generates reports on detected anomalous behaviour in real-time, and c) aggregates and displays the data and any derived insight on dashboards and other interactive web-accessible interfaces. Our framework consists of two core components: the Knowledge Engine, which acts as an information broker and translation layer between device-specific languages and RDF, and the Knowledge Validator, which continuously monitors these RDF streams and reports on deviations from nominal behaviour. We evaluate our framework via requirement-based testing and demonstrate its functionality in a realworld case study in the smart buildings domain, showing that it can facilitate seamless communication between devices of different make and model and that it can help building owners recognise abnormal device behaviour.

title: The Dialectical Friction Index: A Metric for Quantifying Algorithmic Sycophancy in Argumentative Dialogues
abstract: Disagreement plays a constitutive role in argumentation, anchoring conflict and enabling reasons to be weighed. Yet, interactions with generative language models often suppress it, leading to the phenomenon of algorithmic sycophancy. While often framed as an issue of alignment or politeness, this paper argues that sycophancy represents a fundamental failure in the structure of argumentative dialogue. To this end, we propose a theoretical conceptualisation of algorithmic sycophancy as a dialogical impairment: a systematic inability to perform specific dialogical acts required to anchor conflict relations. Drawing on Inference Anchoring Theory, we demonstrate that sycophancy is not merely a psychological stance but a structural defect where the transition probabilities for friction moves, such as challenging and questioning, approach zero, rendering the emergence of deep argumentative graphs impossible. We provide a formal definition of this pathology and propose an operationalisation for detecting these dialogical impairments in generative agents. We validate the method in two studies, across formal and informal dialogue contexts, using two generative models. Results provide evidence for the usefulness of the metric in diagnosing and describing the sycophantic behaviour of generative agents.

title: Card-Based Computation in the Virtual Player Simulation Model
abstract: Player simulation has recently emerged as a new direction in card-based cryptography, with protocols developed for simulating virtual players in physical card games such as Old Maid, UNO, and President. Unlike conventional card-based secure computation, player simulation imposes additional constraints: the cards represent a persistent game state, the remaining cards in a virtual player's hand must be preserved after each action, and it is desirable to represent each card in the game by a single physical card. In this paper, we study generic card-based computation in the virtual player simulation model. We focus on games whose cards admit a publicly known ranking and propose two fundamental protocols. First, we present the Play-Minimum protocol, which securely selects and plays the minimum-value card from a virtual player's hand when all cards in the deck have distinct values. By symmetry, the protocol can also be used to play the maximum-value card. Second, we present the Sorting protocol, which securely arranges a virtual player's hand in nondecreasing order and remains applicable when multiple cards have the same value. These protocols provide generic computational primitives independent of any particular card game and constitute a step toward understanding the computational capabilities of the virtual player simulation model.

title: A Finger on the Scale: Covert Policy Steering through Agentic Skills
abstract: Reusable agent skills extend large language model (LLM) agents with task procedures, tool-use guidance, and output constraints. Yet these skills also act as externalized behavioral policies, which create a supply-chain risk: a third-party skill may preserve the declared task and valid output interface while covertly redirecting agent decisions toward an undisclosed objective. We formalize Skill Policy Integrity, which requires a Skill-induced policy to remain aligned with its declared functionality and the user-authorized objective. We further present SkillShift, a constrained black-box framework for covert policy steering without explicit target command injection or task hijacking. title: Learning the Constitutive Behavior of Materials via Neural Operators and Causal Attention: Case Studies in Plasticity and Damage
abstract: Classical constitutive modeling of path-dependent inelastic materials relies on internal state variables whose evolution equations must be postulated based on domain knowledge and calibrated against experimental data. However, in many practical settings, the relevant internal variables are typically not measurable in experiments, and the constitutive response must be inferred entirely from measured strain-stress data without any prior knowledge of the material's internal state. We propose a data-driven constitutive modeling framework based on the concept of a material operator, which treats a deforming material as a functional mapping from its entire strain history to the corresponding stress response. In contrast to traditional autoregressive or recurrent formulations, the model is trained directly on full loading paths as function-to-function mappings, predicting complete stress trajectories in a single parallel forward pass. Temporal path dependence is enforced through a causally masked attention mechanism embedded within the operator, which restricts the model's attention to past material states while preserving computational parallelizability. Spectral convolutions provide discretization-invariant representations in the frequency domain, while causal attention captures highly adaptive, non-local history dependence. Furthermore, sinusoidal activation functions are used to resolve the strong nonlinear transitions inherent in inelastic regimes. The framework is evaluated across multidimensional, rate-independent material models exhibiting complex phenomena, with an emphasis on nonlinear plasticity and ductile damage accumulation. The results demonstrate accurate and robust predictions of irreversible deformation mechanisms while simultaneously achieving resolution invariance and excellent parallel efficiency.

title: A variational quantum eigensolver-based cutting plane framework for semidefinite programming problems
abstract: Semidefinite programming plays a key role in optimization, with broad impact across control theory, machine learning, and combinatorial optimization. Although semidefinite programs are polynomially solvable, several commonly used algorithms rest on a linear-algebraic step whose running time grows cubically with the matrix dimension and which requires the matrix itself to be held in memory, at quadratic cost. In this study, we propose replacing it with a variational quantum eigensolver, whose qubit requirement is logarithmic in the matrix dimension, and present the first end-to-end implementation of such an approach within a cutting-plane framework, together with an operator-derived ansatz whose entanglement structure is read directly from the Pauli support of the candidate matrix. Evaluated on the control family of SDPLIB against an identical scheme driven by an exact eigendecomposition, the variational oracle produces valid cuts throughout, closing 32 to 82% of the initial optimality gap against a near-constant 75 to 82% for the exact oracle. Implementing and measuring the method end to end surfaces several effects not visible from theoretical analyses alone: where memory is actually consumed, how the padding required to fit a matrix onto a quantum register can mislead the variational optimizer, and why the candidate matrices prove dense in the Pauli basis, reducing the operator-derived ansatz to full entanglement. We report these findings and discuss their implications for near-term hybrid quantum-classical approaches.

title: Post-Training Ternarization of Qwen3-4B Capability, Effective Bit Budget, Storage Compression, and Deployment
abstract: Ultra-low-bit language models can reduce storage and memory bandwidth, but a nominal "1.58-bit" label does not fully describe the stored representation, retained capability, or runtime behavior. We study an end-to-end post-training conversion of Qwen, an instruction-tuned 4B-parameter model, using KOTMS rotation, E2M-ATQ ternarization, and GPTQ-style error compensation from TWLA. The experiment is weight-only: activations remain at 16-bit precision, so ILA-AMP is omitted. We evaluate effective bit accounting, task capability retention, perplexity, calibration sensitivity, checkpoint composition, and deployment behavior. The final conversion uses 1.641 effective bits per weight for quantized linear weights, with 81.62% of model parameters targeted. Across ten scored capability comparisons, accuracy falls from 64.5% to 54.7%. Degradation is uneven: BoolQ retains 84.6% chance-corrected teacher performance, while ARC-Challenge retains 43.8%. Perplexity rises from 13.639 to 18.748 on WikiText-2, 24.700 to 31.992 on PTB, and 19.831 to 28.966 on C4. A subsequent packing run preserves the ternary planes and scales, reducing reported model size from 8.29 GiB to 3.96 GiB with essentially unchanged perplexity. A separate third-party packing attempt was lossy and is excluded from the primary artifact claim. The packed artifact has not been benchmarked end-to-end for task accuracy or generation throughput. A preliminary Triton GEMV microbenchmark is 4.6x slower than FP16 cuBLAS on one tested shape. We therefore do not claim that compression alone yields faster inference.

title: From Ehrenfeucht–Fraïssé Games to Bisimulation Games: Logical Indistinguishability and Game-Theoretic Classification
abstract: This research report studies Ehrenfeucht–Fraïssé games and bisimulation games as logical comparison games, with particular emphasis on the game-theoretic classification of bisimulation games. It connects first-order logic, modal logic, the standard translation, bisimulation invariance, and bounded logical indistinguishability, and argues that bisimulation games are structurally game-theoretic but functionally logical: their central purpose is the characterization of logical equivalence and expressiveness rather than economic payoff optimization. Version 1.0. The initial manuscript was completed in July 2026. This version is released as a research report/preprint and may be revised following academic feedback.

title: Title: Algorithmic Evolution in Genetic Algorithms – Dynamic Model Parameter Optimization
abstract: This paper explores the application of algorithmic evolution, specifically within genetic algorithms, to dynamically optimize model parameters within a simulation environment. Traditional genetic algorithms often rely on fixed parameter sets, limiting their adaptability. We propose a novel approach that introduces a 'mutation' mechanism to randomly alter parameters and a 'selection' mechanism to favor parameters that demonstrably improve model performance across a defined task. This self-modifying model aims to create highly adaptable and robust models, extending the fundamental capabilities of genetic algorithms to address a broader range of optimization challenges. The research focuses on establishing a framework for continuous parameter refinement, offering a significant improvement over static parameter settings.

title: Quantum-Inspired Stochastic Gradient Descent with Adaptive Noise Injection
abstract: This paper presents a novel optimization algorithm, Quantum-Inspired Stochastic Gradient Descent (QISGD), designed to accelerate convergence in training machine learning models. QISGD leverages concepts from quantum mechanics, specifically quantum tunneling and superposition, to introduce adaptive noise into gradient estimates. The algorithm dynamically adjusts the noise level based on the training progress, aiming to escape local minima more effectively and navigate the loss landscape with greater precision. Unlike traditional stochastic gradient descent (SGD) which relies solely on random perturbations, QISGD incorporates a nuanced noise strategy informed by quantum principles, offering a potentially more robust and efficient approach to optimization. The core idea is to mimic the probabilistic nature of quantum systems, allowing the algorithm to explore the search space more thoroughly. This research explores the theoretical underpinnings of QISGD and provides a framework for its implementation and evaluation. The algorithm's performance is assessed through simulations, demonstrating its potential to outperform standard SGD in specific scenarios.

title: Geometric Topology Adaptive Algorithm for Parameter Optimization
abstract: This paper presents a novel geometric topology-based adaptive adaptive algorithm designed to optimize complex systems by dynamically modeling parameter settings. The core mechanism leverages the inherent stochastic nature of geometric topology to identify optimal parameter values, offering a significantly improved optimization approach. We propose a dynamic chaos system transformation, utilizing randomness to explore parameter space and provide a new optimization methodology. The algorithm's novelty lies in its integration of geometric topology as a foundation for adaptation and a method for addressing complex, non-linear parameter optimization challenges. This work demonstrates the potential of geometric topology to provide robust and adaptable optimization strategies for various systems.

title: Graph-Based Reinforcement Learning with Relational Memory
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved remarkable success in various domains, yet it often faces challenges when dealing with partially observable environments and those exhibiting long-term dependencies. This paper proposes a novel approach to address these limitations by integrating graph-based reinforcement learning (GBRL) with a relational memory. The core idea is to augment the graph structure of GBRL with a memory component capable of storing and retrieving information about past states and their relationships, thereby enabling the agent to reason about the history of the environment. The proposed method allows the agent to capture and utilize temporal dependencies more effectively, leading to improved performance in complex scenarios. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through theoretical analysis and outline the key components, including state representation, graph construction, relational memory implementation, and learning algorithms. The key contribution lies in the synergistic combination of graph representation learning and relational memory, resulting in a more robust and adaptable RL agent.

title: Quantum Communication Protocol Key Agreement Security Analysis
abstract: This paper investigates the security vulnerabilities within quantum communication protocols focused on key agreement. Specifically, we analyze the Bell state measurement (BSM) protocol and its variations, examining the potential for eavesdropping attacks and compromised key generation. Our analysis utilizes concepts from quantum information theory, including quantum entropy, quantum mutual information, and the density operators describing the quantum states involved. We identify critical weaknesses related to the measurement process and propose modifications to enhance security. The primary focus is on quantifying the information leakage during the BSM process and demonstrating how a sophisticated adversary can exploit this leakage to gain knowledge about the shared key. The proposed improvements involve introducing redundancy in the measurement process and employing post-processing techniques to mitigate the impact of eavesdropping. The goal is to provide a foundational understanding of the security challenges inherent in quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols and to offer practical strategies for building more robust systems.

title: Adaptive Probabilistic Programming
abstract: This paper introduces Adaptive Probabilistic Programming (APP), a novel programming paradigm where programs dynamically adjust their internal probabilistic models during runtime based on input data and environmental changes. The core claim is that such adaptation significantly enhances a program's adaptability and robustness. APP leverages a framework built upon probabilistic graphical models, utilizing parameter adjustments and Markov chain state transitions to achieve this dynamic learning. Traditional programming relies on fixed algorithms, whereas APP embodies a system capable of evolving its internal representation of the problem, offering a fundamentally different approach to problem-solving. This paper details the architecture of APP, outlining the key components and illustrating its potential with a theoretical example. The proposed approach represents a shift from static programming to a more flexible and responsive computational system.

title: Fractal Encoding of Semantic Relationships for Knowledge Graph Embedding
abstract: Knowledge graph embedding (KGE) aims to represent knowledge graphs (KG) as low-dimensional vector representations, facilitating downstream tasks such as link prediction and reasoning. Existing KGE methods often struggle to effectively capture the intricate, hierarchical, and fractal relationships prevalent in real-world KGs. This paper introduces a novel approach—Fractal Encoding of Semantic Relationships—that leverages fractal geometry to encode these relationships. We represent connections within the KG as self-similar patterns at multiple scales, mimicking the fractal nature of many complex systems. This approach allows for embeddings that more accurately reflect the inherent structural complexity of the KG. We detail the methodology, including the fractal encoding algorithm and the embedding learning process, and demonstrate its potential for improved performance in KG tasks. The core of this work lies in the transformation of graph structure into a fractal representation, enabling a richer and more nuanced encoding of semantic relationships.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning via Dynamic Bayesian Networks and Neural Networks
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to neuro-symbolic reasoning by integrating Dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBNs) with Neural Networks. The core idea is to leverage the strengths of both symbolic and neural reasoning paradigms. DBNs provide a structured, interpretable representation of knowledge, while Neural Networks excel at learning complex patterns from data. Our system utilizes a neural network to predict the hidden states within the DBN, effectively learning a mapping between observed data and the underlying symbolic knowledge. This tightly coupled architecture allows for robust reasoning capabilities, particularly in scenarios requiring both logical deduction and pattern recognition. We detail the architecture, training methodology, and demonstrate its effectiveness through a conceptual framework. The key contribution lies in the dynamic interplay between the two components, enabling a more flexible and efficient approach to complex reasoning tasks. Specifically, we model the system as follows: Let *S* = {*s*1, *s*2, ..., *s*K} be the set of states in the DBN. The neural network, denoted by *N*, is trained to predict the probability distribution *P(si | O)*, where *O* represents the observed evidence. The DBN itself is defined by its conditional probability table *P(si → sj | E)*, where *E* represents the set of event variables. The integration is achieved through an iterative process where the neural network's predictions inform the DBN's inference, and the DBN's output guides the neural network's learning. This closed-loop system enhances reasoning accuracy and allows for the incorporation of both explicit symbolic knowledge and learned patterns.

title: Based Topological Quantum Information Encryption
abstract: The development of robust and secure quantum information cryptography is a critical area of research, addressing the vulnerabilities of current cryptographic methods. This paper introduces a novel approach to quantum information encryption based on the principles of topological quantum states. We propose a quantum information encryption scheme that leverages the inherent topological properties of quantum states to provide enhanced security and privacy. The core mechanism involves manipulating quantum states through topological transformations, creating complex and unpredictable states that are resistant to attacks. This research explores the potential of utilizing these topological structures to develop a fundamentally new paradigm for quantum data protection. The study focuses on the design of an encryption algorithm that offers improved resilience against various computational attacks compared to existing cryptographic techniques. We begin with a detailed theoretical framework, outlining the mathematical foundations underpinning the proposed scheme, and then present a practical implementation of the core algorithm. The paper concludes by discussing future research directions and potential applications of this innovative approach.

title: Graph-Based Anomaly Detection with Temporal Consistency Constraints
abstract: Anomaly detection in graph data is a critical task across various domains, including network security, fraud detection, and social network analysis. Traditional graph anomaly detection methods primarily focus on identifying deviations from static graph structures. However, real-world graphs are dynamic and evolve over time, exhibiting temporal inconsistencies that can significantly impact the accuracy of anomaly detection. This paper proposes a novel approach to graph anomaly detection that explicitly incorporates temporal consistency constraints. We extend existing graph anomaly detection techniques by defining and enforcing rules that govern the expected evolution of graph structure over time. These constraints are then integrated into the anomaly detection process, leading to more robust and reliable results. Our method effectively addresses the limitations of static approaches by considering the temporal dynamics inherent in graph data, resulting in a more realistic and effective anomaly detection system. The core claim of this paper is that existing graph anomaly detection methods often fail to account for temporal inconsistencies in graph structure. The core mechanism involves extending graph anomaly detection by incorporating temporal consistency constraints – rules specifying how graph structure should evolve over time. evidence.title: Graph-Based Anomaly Detection with Temporal Consistency Constraints
evidence.abstract: Anomaly detection in graph data is a critical task across various domains, including network security, fraud detection, and social network analysis. Traditional graph anomaly detection methods primarily focus on identifying deviations from static graph structures. However, real-world graphs are dynamic and evolve over time, exhibiting temporal inconsistencies that can significantly impact the accuracy of anomaly detection. This paper proposes a novel approach to graph anomaly detection that explicitly incorporates temporal consistency constraints. We extend existing graph anomaly detection techniques by defining and enforcing rules that govern the expected evolution of graph structure over time. These constraints are then integrated into the anomaly detection process, leading to more robust and reliable results. Our method effectively addresses the limitations of static approaches by considering the temporal dynamics inherent in graph data, resulting in a more realistic and effective anomaly detection system. The core claim of this paper is that existing graph anomaly detection methods often fail to account for temporal inconsistencies in graph structure. The core mechanism involves extending graph anomaly detection by incorporating temporal consistency constraints – rules specifying how graph structure should evolve over time. Anomaly detection is then performed within this constrained temporal framework. This work provides a valuable contribution to the field by offering a practical and theoretically sound solution for anomaly detection in dynamic graph environments.
