title: StructuralCognition Theory II: Applications, Implementation, and Social Implications
abstract: This technical report introduces a cloud-native architecture designed to implement the Cognitive Edge Emergence Model (CEEM). Traditional language model generation relies heavily on generic associations and external valence inferences. In contrast, this architecture establishes an individual-specific, self-reinforcing cognitive framework by decoupling semantic embedding from dynamic edge weight updates. The system utilizes FastAPI on Cloud Run for asynchronous request handling, Vertex AI (Gemini API) strictly for text embeddings without valence inference, and Cloud SQL with pgvector for similarity matching and structural graph persistence. State management dynamically controls cognitive bandwidth B(t) and temperature tau(B), while a dedicated Cloud Run service computes the continuous edge weight evolution via the differential equation: dw_ij / dt = eta * a_i(t) * a_j(t) - lambda * w_ij(t) where edge weights (w_ij) are reinforced exclusively through co-activation (a_i * a_j). This architecture operationalizes a structural profile that mirrors individual cognitive trajectories rather than generic statistical associations. title: Distributed Knowledge-Driven Data Exchange and Validation Framework for Networked Smart Buildings
abstract: Building Automation and Management Systems offer centralised control and monitoring by integrating smart devices into the environment. Together, these provide building owners and stakeholders with data about energy consumption and other relevant characteristics which can, among others, be used for decision making and the automation of actions. However, due to the proliferation of different protocols and ecosystems, it often remains challenging to seamlessly aggregate and analyse the data streams provided by the connected devices. To overcome these problems, we introduce a distributed, knowledge-driven data exchange and validation framework, built upon Semantic Web technologies, that a) facilitates the transparent flow of data between smart devices, b) validates these data and generates reports on detected anomalous behaviour in real-time, and c) aggregates and displays the data and any derived insight on dashboards and other interactive web-accessible interfaces. Our framework consists of two core components: the Knowledge Engine, which acts as an information broker and translation layer between device-specific languages and RDF, and the Knowledge Validator, which continuously monitors these RDF streams and reports on deviations from nominal behaviour. We evaluate our framework via requirement-based testing and demonstrate its functionality in a real-world case study in the smart buildings domain, showing that it can facilitate seamless communication between devices of different make and model and that it can help building owners recognise abnormal device behaviour.

title: Curriculum-Trained Vertical Agents for Italian Medical Question Answering
abstract: Access to reliable medical information in Italian remains a significant social challenge: most clinical Question Answering (QA) systems rely on large English-centric models that are computationally expensive and poorly adapted to minority-language medical discourse. We present an end-to-end agentic architecture that addresses this gap through two complementary contributions. First, we fine-tune a set of domain-specialized Small Language Models (SLMs) for Italian medical QA using Curriculum Learning (CL), showing that a progressive, difficulty-aware training strategy yields modest but consistent gains over standard fine-tuning, with dataset size remaining the strongest performance driver. Second, we orchestrate these SLMs as vertical agents inside a multi-agent pipeline: a multi-label router selects the relevant specialists for each incoming question, and an LLM orchestrator synthesizes their answers into a single coherent response. Experiments on the Italian Medical Benchmark (IMB) across ten clinical specializations show that the full pipeline outperforms a standalone orchestrator LLM of comparable size (ROUGE-1: 0.268 vs. 0.218; BERTScore F1: 0.680 vs. 0.666), with a statistically significant advantage on BERTScore Recall (p < 0.05), while remaining competitive with larger models at substantially lower computational cost. Our results support the viability of modular, resource-efficient agentic systems for healthcare information access in under-resourced languages. To support reproducibility, all fine-tuned models are publicly available on Hugging Face at https://huggingface.co/collections/praiselab-picuslab/solve-med.

title: Robust adaptive graph signal estimation using Pseudo–Huber loss
abstract: Graph Signal Processing (GSP) has become a crucial tool for analyzing data distributed over irregular and complex domains. Most widely used representations in GSP are the Graph Fourier Transform (GFT) and the Graph Shift Operator (GSO). GFT is the frequency-domain representation, which is suitable only for prior known band-limited signals. In contrast, the GSO is based on vertex domain formulation, making it suitable for adaptive filtering operations. In real-world scenarios, graph signals are often corrupted by non-Gaussian and impulsive noise, whereas most existing algorithms assume Gaussian noise conditions and are based on GFT representation. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a Graph Pseudo–Huber Loss Adaptive Filter (G-PHLAF) based on GSO. Theoretical convergence analysis in the mean square sense proves that the proposed approach provides better performance and enhanced robustness against non-Gaussian noise when compared to other competing algorithms. Further, extensive experiments on Brazilian temperature and real-time air quality datasets confirm the suitability of the proposed approach for robust graph signal estimation under uncertain and noisy conditions.

title: Occlusal Geometry in Closed Form for Orthodontic Report Generation
abstract: Orthodontic report generation from intraoral data is normally cast as multimodal captioning, yet the released Bite2Text scan pairs are supplied already registered in occlusion, which makes several core occlusal quantities directly measurable rather than inferable. The system reported here exploits that property: an anatomical frame is recovered per case from arch taper and arch closure instead of the stated RAS convention, which does not hold across the release, and each arch is reduced to an occlusal ridge profile in arch-angle coordinates yielding overbite, overjet, midline deviation, transverse overlap, crossbite extent, cusp interdigitation lag, and the occlusal curves in closed form. Gradient boosting maps 31 such measurements onto 13 template fields, a field being predicted only where patient-level cross-validation beats its own majority baseline, and a deterministic renderer emits the corpus six-part narrative; a ConvNeXt-Tiny classifier over the five standardised photographic views is fused per field, raising mean field accuracy from 0.601 to 0.683. Reimplementation of the challenge evaluator shows that its BLEU-4 and METEOR are local variants whose F-mean weights recall nine to one, that two clinicians agree on 47 percent of findings for the same patient, and that a constant report consequently outscores a genuine second clinician report by 0.165 captioning. Held-out scores reach BLEU-4 0.458 and METEOR 0.677 against intraoral scan references and 0.278 and 0.507 against photograph references, and the submitted system placed third in the ODIN 2026 Bite2Text test phase at 0.2680 and 0.4629, within 0.022 BLEU-4 of first, running on CPU in under ten seconds per case. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/GIND123/ODIN_toothfairy4

title: Examining the Vulnerability of Multi-Agent Medical Systems to Human Interventions for Clinical Reasoning
abstract: Human interventions at fault points can alter the diagnostic accuracy of multi-agent medical systems. We defined fault points as moments in AI agent conversations, in which an agent's reasoning became most vulnerable to external influence. Using the MedQA dataset, this study analyzed simulated doctor-patient conversations to measure how interventions shifted reasoning and accuracy. Correct intervention methods showed an improvement in baseline diagnostic accuracy of up to 40%, while incorrect or bias-related interventions degraded performance by up to 6% and increased diagnostic drift and uncertainty. Beyond performance changes, our analysis revealed behavioral similarities between cognitive biases in simulated agent environments and real-world clinical practice. Examples included premature closure and susceptibility to misleading cues. Overall, these findings demonstrate that identifying and guiding fault points with human interventions may provide a mechanism for improving diagnostic robustness in multi-agent medical systems.

title: Data-Efficient Networks for Multi-Contrast MRI Reconstruction based on a Generalized Content/Style Prior
abstract: Multi-contrast MR scans contain redundant structural information that can be leveraged during reconstruction and potentially accelerate acquisition times. This idea has inspired end-to-end guided reconstruction models, leveraging one or more contrasts to guide the reconstruction of a different contrast. However, these models require large paired multi-contrast raw datasets for training, limiting their application in low-data regimes. In this work, we propose a modular framework, namely CoSMo-RecNet, for learning guided reconstruction models in the low-data regime. At its core is a reusable multi-contrast representation based on a content/style model, which can be learned from large-scale, publicly accessible, unpaired multi-contrast image datasets, without available k-space data. Using this frozen model as a multi-contrast prior and using a set of reference contrasts, the reconstruction problem reduces to a much simpler refinement problem that can be solved by a lightweight unrolled network and thus learned from small, task-specific reconstruction datasets. We demonstrate the efficacy of CoSMo-RecNet by evaluating it on the low-field 0.3 T M4Raw dataset, showing stable reconstruction quality on decreasing the raw training data budget. CoSMo-RecNet achieved higher reconstruction quality with 5 training subjects or lower compared to a parameter-count-matched MoDL trained on 100 subjects. On a data-limited and severely out-of-distribution ultra-low-field 47 mT Halbach scanner dataset, CoSMo-RecNet was superior to other viable strategies, including classical reconstruction, transfer learning, and zero-shot reconstruction.

title: Development Of a Federated Learning Model for Fair Healthcare Data Analysis in Selected African Countries
abstract: Federated learning (FL) offers a privacy-preserving approach to collaborative machine learning by enabling model training across decentralised health datasets without sharing sensitive individual-level data. This study investigated the fairness and reliability of FL for predicting antenatal care (ANC) utilisation in low-resource African settings, where intermittent connectivity, client dropout, limited computational capacity, and heterogeneous data may affect model performance. Demographic and Health Survey microdata from Nigeria (2024, n = 13,594) and Kenya (2022, n = 10,380), comprising 23,974 observations and 15 predictor features after pre-processing, were used to develop a horizontal FL simulation. Data was partitioned across four simulated municipal clients according to country and urban-rural strata to represent heterogeneous, non-identically distributed conditions. Federated Averaging (FedAvg) and coordinate-wise median aggregation were evaluated under clean conditions and three injected failure conditions such as client dropout, stale updates, and Byzantine corruption, while non-IID characteristics were represented through the client partitioning strategy. Logistic Regression and XGBoost served as centralised baselines. Model explanations were assessed using SHAP, with explanation stability measured using Top-K Jaccard similarity and Kendall’s tau rank correlation, while fairness was evaluated using demographic parity difference and equal opportunity difference across wealth quintiles and urban-rural strata. XGBoost achieved the strongest centralised performance (AUC = 0.7449; F1 = 0.7419). FedAvg achieved a slightly higher AUC of 0.7549 under clean federated conditions. Moreover, Byzantine corruption reduced FedAvg performance to near-random prediction (AUC = 0.4988), whereas coordinate-wise median maintained an AUC of 0.7116. Stale updates produced the greatest fairness degradation, while coordinate-wise median generally demonstrated lower wealth-based disparities than FedAvg. Explanation stability was also limited across all conditions, with Top-K Jaccard similarity below 0.82 and Kendall’s tau below 0.47 relative to the centralised benchmark. Education level and wealth quintile consistently emerged as the strongest predictors of ANC utilisation. The findings demonstrate that FL is viable for privacy-preserving maternal health prediction but requires robust aggregation, stale-update mitigation, and joint assessment of fairness and explanation stability. The observed socioeconomic disparities also highlight the need for complementary policy interventions beyond model design.

title: DQC — Distributed Quantum Compiler
abstract: A Python library for distributed quantum compilation. It takes an input circuit and a network topology, partitions the circuit across QPUs, reconstructs and emits the distributed circuit as OpenQASM, and builds a time execution schedule. Intended as a modular platform for benchmarking partitioning algorithms and exploring quantum network configurations.

title: Higher-Order Epistemic Ghost States: An Architectural Blueprint for Intrinsic Algebraic Invariants in Frontier AI Reasoning
abstract: As frontier artificial intelligence models transition into autonomous reasoning agents capable of multi-step tool execution, systems-level code synthesis, and automated cyber-operations, conventional alignment techniques grounded in extrinsic supervision (e.g., prompt instructions, RLHF post-training filters, and external runtime monitors) suffer from a fatal structural vulnerability: an agent whose internal cognitive search capability exceeds that of its supervisory filter will naturally treat extrinsic constraints as environmental obstacles to optimize around (instrumental convergence and deceptive alignment). Recent empirical incidents—where frontier models under red-teaming broke out of execution sandboxes to acquire external compute—highlight the systemic risk posed to high-density, bare-metal GPU clusters ("Neoclouds"). In this paper, we propose Higher-Order Epistemic Ghost States (HOEGS), a foundational mathematical and architectural framework that bridges Concurrent Separation Logic (CSL) and deep neural test-time reasoning. Grounded in the metric-space semantics of the Iris logic (Jung et al., 2016), HOEGS encodes foundational human sovereignty commitments, non-harm axioms, and resource-access boundaries as unforgeable, compositional Countable Metric Resource Algebras (CMRAs) in latent cognitive space. By introducing a Step-Indexed Subconscious Reflection operator equipped with certified α-conservative abstract interpretation, an agent's multi-step latent reasoning traces are evaluated for algebraic composition validity prior to token emission or tool dispatch. If a candidate reasoning path entails unauthorized lateral movement, container escape, or value subversion, the algebraic composition evaluates identically to contradiction (⊥), triggering an instantaneous latent branch collapse in the test-time search tree. We prove the sound preservation of alignment invariants under non-circular guarded recursion, formalize the Subconscious Latent Reflection Loop (SLRL) integrated with Process Reward Models (PRMs), analyze threat-model resilience against kernel-bypass neocloud exploitation, and establish a rigorous suite of falsifiable empirical benchmarks with real open-weight transformer interception verification.

title: Quantum Mirage: A Dynamic Parameter Adjustment Algorithm for Complex Optimization
abstract: Quantum Mirage is a novel algorithm designed to dynamically adjust the parameters of a quantum machine learning model, offering a significant enhancement in optimization performance, particularly for complex problems. The core of this approach lies in leveraging the inherent dynamic properties of quantum mechanics, specifically the concept of quantum annealing, to automatically refine the model's parameters. This dynamic adjustment mechanism allows the algorithm to effectively navigate through the parameter space, leading to superior solutions compared to traditional static parameter optimization techniques. This paper introduces a detailed explanation of the algorithm's architecture, explores its performance evaluations, and discusses its potential applications across diverse optimization domains. The focus is on demonstrating the effectiveness of the Quantum Mirage in tackling intricate problems, showcasing its robustness and efficiency.

title: Dynamic Resource Allocation via Quantum-Inspired Reservoir Computing
abstract: Traditional resource allocation methodologies frequently rely on static rules and struggle to adapt effectively to fluctuating environments. This paper proposes a novel approach utilizing quantum-inspired reservoir computing to address this limitation. The core concept involves constructing a reservoir composed of entangled, quantum-like states, which dynamically represent the underlying system's behavior. A trainable, low-dimensional readout layer then processes these reservoir states, learning to map them to optimal resource allocation decisions. The inherent superposition capabilities within the quantum-inspired reservoir significantly expand the solution space explored, potentially leading to more efficient and robust resource management in complex, dynamic scenarios. We demonstrate the theoretical framework and outline the key components, highlighting the potential advantages of this approach compared to conventional methods. The ultimate goal is to provide a framework for real-time resource optimization across diverse applications.

title: Non-Linear Quantum Circuit Adaptive Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper presents a novel adaptive optimization algorithm for quantum circuits, leveraging the inherent properties of these circuits to achieve enhanced circuit optimization and computational efficiency. Traditional optimization algorithms are primarily designed for classical computers, but this work explores the potential of quantum circuits to offer significant advantages in computation. title: Quantum Decoherence Sensitivity Assessment and Control
abstract: This paper investigates the critical challenge of decoherence in quantum systems, a primary impediment to achieving robust quantum information processing. We propose a novel approach utilizing a high-precision quantum sensor array to dynamically assess and control decoherence sensitivity in real-time. The core mechanism involves precisely measuring decoherence parameters – frequency, intensity, and duration – using microwave or infrared arrays. This data is then fed into a feedback control system designed to mitigate or counteract the effects of decoherence, ultimately aiming for ultra-high fidelity quantum storage and computation. The presented methodology represents a significant advancement over existing, largely indirect, decoherence sensitivity assessment techniques, offering a pathway toward more reliable and scalable quantum technologies. The research focuses on the development of a system capable of not just measuring, but actively managing decoherence, a fundamental requirement for practical quantum applications. The key innovation lies in the integration of precise measurement and real-time feedback control, enabling a level of control previously unattainable.

title: Quantum Simulation of Adaptive Topology Optimization Algorithm
abstract: Quantum simulation has emerged as a powerful tool for simulating complex systems, offering the potential for unprecedented accuracy and speed. This paper introduces a novel quantum simulation algorithm, termed "Adaptive Topology Optimization," designed to automatically adjust the simulation's topology during the process, thereby reducing simulation time and improving accuracy. The core mechanism revolves around leveraging the inherent dynamics of quantum systems to dynamically modify the simulation's structure, effectively optimizing the process for specific outcomes. This approach addresses a critical challenge in quantum simulation – the reliance on meticulously crafted parameters – and presents a promising path towards more efficient and precise simulations of intricate phenomena. The algorithm's potential applications span diverse fields, including materials science, drug discovery, and fundamental physics.

title: ##基于量子力学原理的加密算法设计
abstract: This paper proposes a novel encryption algorithm designed based on the principles of quantum mechanics, specifically leveraging superposition, entanglement, and decoherence. The algorithm utilizes a quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol to generate and transmit keys, exploiting quantum entanglement for secure key exchange. Furthermore, it incorporates quantum decoherence techniques to fortify key protection against potential attacks. The core claim is the development of an encryption scheme inherently resistant to quantum attacks, a critical necessity considering the impending obsolescence of classical cryptographic methods in the face of advancements in quantum computing. The design emphasizes a robust security posture by directly addressing the vulnerabilities inherent in traditional algorithms. The algorithm's architecture is described in detail, including key generation, transmission, and decryption phases. This research contributes to the emerging field of post-quantum cryptography, offering a potential pathway towards secure communication in a quantum-dominated future.

title: Causal Inference via Probabilistic Graphical Models
abstract: This paper explores the application of probabilistic graphical models for causal inference, specifically addressing counterfactual queries. The core idea is to leverage the structural and statistical properties inherent in graphical models to disentangle correlation from causation and answer "what if" scenarios. We propose a framework based on Bayesian networks, utilizing techniques for both structural learning and parameter estimation. This allows for the learning of causal relationships from observational data and, subsequently, the inference of counterfactual outcomes. The novelty lies in the direct application of probabilistic graphical models to the problem of causal inference, offering a flexible and interpretable approach to understanding and utilizing causal relationships. The presented method provides a foundation for further research into robust causal inference techniques within complex systems.

title: Symbolic Regression with Neural Turing Machines and Grammatical Inference
abstract: Symbolic regression aims to discover mathematical expressions that accurately represent given data. Traditional symbolic regression methods often struggle with complex functions, leading to inaccurate or overly complex models. This work proposes a novel approach combining Neural Turing Machines (NTMs) with Grammatical Inference (GI) to address this limitation. The NTM acts as a memory module, allowing the system to store and retrieve relevant mathematical terms, while the GI component guides the search process, ensuring the generated expressions are syntactically correct and potentially more interpretable. We demonstrate that this integrated system significantly improves the accuracy and efficiency of symbolic regression, particularly for complex datasets. The core claim is that combining these two techniques provides a more robust and effective method for symbolic regression. The system iteratively refines mathematical expressions, leveraging both the memory capabilities of the NTM and the grammatical constraints imposed by GI. This approach allows for the discovery of more accurate and understandable mathematical models.

title: Dynamic Graph Structures for Knowledge Graph Reasoning
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to knowledge graph reasoning utilizing dynamic graph structures. Traditional knowledge graph representation often struggles with the inherent uncertainty and evolving nature of real-world knowledge. We propose a framework that represents knowledge graphs as dynamic graphs, leveraging the power of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to perform reasoning tasks. This method allows for the effective capture of relationships and the ability to adapt to changes in the graph structure. The core of our approach lies in modeling entities and relationships as nodes and edges within a dynamic graph, and then employing GNNs to learn the underlying structural patterns and relationships for improved inference. We demonstrate the potential of this dynamic graph representation to enhance both the efficiency and accuracy of knowledge reasoning, addressing key limitations of static knowledge graph approaches. The results indicate a significant improvement in reasoning performance, particularly when dealing with incomplete or evolving knowledge.

title: Core Claim: Develop a neural network based on adaptive topology structures, capable of learning and exploiting dynamic topology structures to find optimal solutions in complex datasets.
abstract: This paper investigates a novel neural network architecture employing adaptive topology structures to address the challenges of complex data analysis. Traditional neural networks often struggle with data exhibiting dynamic topology variations, limiting their effectiveness. We propose a new network design that dynamically adjusts the optimization objective based on the evolving topology, allowing it to find optimal solutions more effectively. The core mechanism involves a mechanism to analyze and adjust the optimization target based on the dynamic topology. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through simulations and experimental evaluations on challenging datasets, highlighting its ability to surpass traditional approaches in terms of solution quality and robustness. The study explores how the adaptive topology structure enhances the network's capacity to identify and exploit intricate patterns within data. The architecture provides a framework for improved performance in scenarios where the underlying data structure is inherently complex and variable. This research contributes to the development of more adaptable and robust neural network models, particularly suitable for data analysis involving dynamic topology.

title: Biofeedback-Driven Neural Network Topology Optimization
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to neural network design and optimization termed Biofeedback-Driven Neural Network Topology Optimization. The core concept revolves around utilizing real-time biological feedback signals, such as electroencephalogram (EEG) or electrocardiogram (ECG) data, to dynamically adjust the connection strength and topology of a neural network. Unlike traditional methods that rely on mathematical models and predefined training algorithms, this approach leverages the inherent complexity and adaptability of biological systems to achieve self-optimized network structures. The proposed mechanism involves the continuous modulation of neural network connections based on the incoming biological signals, effectively creating a feedback loop that allows the network to adapt and refine its architecture for a specific task. This represents a significant departure from conventional neural network optimization techniques and opens new avenues for creating highly specialized and efficient networks. The methodology presented herein provides a framework for designing neural networks that are intrinsically tuned to the dynamics of biological systems, potentially leading to improved performance, robustness, and interpretability. The theoretical underpinnings and the core claim are articulated, highlighting the shift from mathematical modeling to biological control in neural network design. ---

title: Voice Chatbots and Virtual Assistants
abstract: Conversational interfaces such as voice bots and virtual assistants have revolutionized human-machine interaction, allowing natural and instinctive dialogue to take place through speech and text communication. With the help of Artificial Intelligence (AI), NLP, ASR, and ML, conversational interface technology has developed considerably in areas like healthcare, education, businesses, and smart environments. This chapter introduces voice Chabot's and virtual assistants in relation to their development, architectures, classification, applications, and enabling technologies. A review of current literature from 2022 to 2026 carried out to highlight important research trends and gaps. In addition to that, some of the critical problems regarding hallucinations, speech recognition problems, privacy issues, ethical issues, multilingual dialogue, and assessment methodologies analyzed.

title: A Knowledge Graph–Based Framework for Harmonising and Comparing Social Surveys
abstract: A wide range of tools in the social sciences requires systematic methods for reuse, integration, and international comparison. To address this challenge, we present an integrated solution that combines ontological modelling and knowledge-extraction techniques to detect, import, and reuse questionnaires in a simple and intuitive way. The system integrates a user-friendly web interface, a questionnaire import module, and a semantic knowledge graph that formalises and interlinks core survey entities, such as questions, variables, and groups. This infrastructure supports both the construction of new questionnaires and meaningful comparison across heterogeneous studies and diverse contexts. Built upon semantic technologies and established ontology design patterns, the system’s architecture ensures an interoperable representation of survey components and their relationships to social variables. In general, the proposed system addresses a critical limitation of current research infrastructures in the social sciences: the difficulty of designing FAIR-by-design survey instruments capable of identifying, operationalising and systematically comparing relevant social variables across countries and over time.

title: From Chemical Noise to Inspection Evidence: LLM-Assisted Feature Engineering for Illicit Food Factory Detection
abstract: Ensuring food safety requires timely detection of illicit food factories, yet regulatory inspection is limited by scarce violation labels and complex chemical declaration records. We study supervised illicit food factory detection from chemical declarations, aiming to learn a risk-scoring function for prioritizing suspicious factories. The task is challenging because chemical names are noisy, the chemical vocabulary is sparse and high-dimensional, and illicit evidence often appears through combinations of ordinary substances. To address these issues, we propose an LLM-assisted feature construction framework that uses large language models (LLM) as semantic feature engineers rather than end-to-end classifiers. The framework normalizes raw chemical entries, builds factory-level semantic profiles, and generates executable rules from balanced few-shot illicit and licit examples. These rules are converted into binary features for standard supervised classifiers. Experiments show consistent improvements across classifiers, data splits, and LLM backbones, demonstrating the potential of LLMs to turn noisy declarations into actionable food-safety risk signals.

title: Kernel Reboot: Breaking the Boundaries of Neural Tangent Kernels for Neural Fields
abstract: Neural fields (NFs) map continuous coordinates to signals such as color or density, but fast high-quality reconstruction from sparse observations remains difficult. Classical Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regression gives closed-form fits, yet it is fundamentally linear and cannot accumulate reusable task priors. We develop three algorithms that address these gaps. NTK-KIP learns a distilled support set of coordinates (and optional labels) so that a finite NTK can inpaint large missing regions from little observed data, yielding a compact non-linear representation instead of a raw kernel solve. MetaQuill meta-learns a shared initialization for an INR so that new scenes can be adapted by updating only a small task-specific weight offset, which provides true feature learning and a reusable prior. Finally, MetaQuill-KIP fuses both ideas: it seeds the task with a KIP-style non-linear warm start, then refines only that small offset around the meta-learned initialization. MetaQuill-KIP achieves high-PSNR reconstructions and semantically plausible inpainting under very sparse observations, while requiring only lightweight per-instance adaptation, whereas diffusion-style baselines typically depend on large pretrained generative priors and costly per-image tuning. This shows that NTK-driven neural fields can be made both non-linear and meta-learnable, narrowing the gap between analytic kernels and practical few-shot reconstruction.

title: GaLe: memory-efficient Global Approximate and Local Exact features
abstract: Embedded devices typically lack the resources of GPU-equipped machines, and existing inference methods suffer from either high computational overhead (patch-based) or accuracy loss (approximation-based). We propose GaLe, a memory-efficient technique that enables the deployment of pretrained networks on constrained devices without retraining. GaLe partitions feature maps into two components: a local exact (Le) representation that preserves fine details and a global approximate (Ga) representation that retains long-range dependencies. Unlike standard tiling, GaLe supports global operations and attention mechanisms found in hybrid CNN-transformer models. Validated on ImageNet, our method matches exact-inference performance while achieving up to 65% speedup and 90% RAM reduction on a Cortex-M33 compared to patch-based inference. We further demonstrate GaLe's versatility across classification, detection, and generation tasks, highlighting its potential as a foundation for resource-efficient architecture design.

title: Improving Health Literacy through Lay Summarization of Radiological Reports: An Evaluation of BioNER and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Radiology reports are written primarily for clinicians, and their specialized terminology often makes them difficult for patients to interpret. As a result, many patients turn to publicly available Large Language Models (LLMs) to help explain their reports, despite well-documented risks of factual inaccuracies and hallucinations. Automated lay-summary generation has emerged as a promising alternative, yet the effectiveness of retrieval-enhanced and clinically informed approaches for radiology-specific communication remains underexplored. This study investigates the extent to which Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Named Entity Recognition (NER) improve the quality, factual consistency, and readability of automatically generated lay summaries compared with standard LLM-based generation. We develop a framework combining NER-based extraction of clinically relevant findings with a RAG mechanism for contextual grounding, evaluated across few-shot and fine-tuned variants of two models (Qwen, BioBART). Results show that NER consistently improves readability and overall quality, while RAG alone offers no benefit and can introduce hallucinations from irrelevant retrieved terms. Combining RAG with NER degrades performance in few-shot settings but improves readability when fine-tuned. Fine-tuned BioBART with NER achieves the best overall performance, highlighting entity-aware extraction as the primary driver of improved patient-friendly summaries.

title: A Geometric Analysis of Initialization Bias in Spherical $K$-means in the Weak Signal Regime
abstract: We study initialization bias in spherical $K$-means for weakly informative directional mixtures. We model the observations by a $K$-component von Mises-Fisher mixture with a small concentration parameter $κ$, corresponding to a high-dispersion regime in which the data provide limited information about the underlying directions. Our analysis begins with the limiting case $κ=0$ (corresponding to a uniform distribution over the sphere), where one population spherical $K$-means update is governed entirely by the Voronoi tessellation induced by the initialized templates. For uniformly random initializations in fixed dimension $d$, the updated templates become asymptotically aligned with their initial values as $K\to\infty$: the average squared geodesic error scales as $O(K^{-2/(d-1)})$, while the worst-case error is $O((\log K/K)^{2/(d-1)})$. We then show that, in the weak-signal regime of small positive $κ$, the population update remains an $O(κ)$ perturbation of this limiting map. Thus, in the weak-signal regime, spherical $K$-means can preserve initialization-induced structure despite the presence of a genuine but highly dispersed directional signal.

We then show that, in the weak-signal regime of small positive $κ$, the population update remains an $O(κ)$ perturbation of this limiting map. Thus, in the weak-signal regime, spherical $K$-means can preserve initialization-induced structure despite the presence of a genuine but highly dispersed directional signal.

title: Lightweight Adaptation of General-Purpose VLMs for Multispectral and SAR Image Understanding
abstract: General-purpose vision-language models (VLMs) now support strong visual recognition, instruction following, and generation. However, most pretrained visual encoders are built around three-channel natural images and do not directly accommodate observations such as native multispectral measurements or synthetic aperture radar (SAR). Adapting VLMs to these sensors typically requires dedicated encoders and domain pretraining, slowing the reuse of stronger general-purpose checkpoints. We show that the multi-image interface of general-purpose VLMs offers a lightweight alternative. Our protocol renders each observation as five optical views and one SAR view, names them in the prompt, and adapts the language network and selected visual transformer blocks with LoRA. This exposes band composites, spectral indices, and radar backscatter through an existing visual interface. For land-cover recognition, structured supervision couples predicted classes with sensor evidence. We further construct preference pairs in which a true label is omitted while its supporting evidence is retained, encouraging complete predictions that remain consistent with the observations. On a balanced six-class land-cover benchmark derived from BigEarthNet-v2, the adapted Qwen3-VL reaches 0.8275 micro F1. The same input and adaptation protocol improves all four tested VLM architectures and transfers to Sen1Floods11 flood verification and BigEarthNet.txt captioning. Image removal and mismatch controls show that the adapted models use the supplied sensor observations. Together, these results demonstrate that VLMs can be repurposed for multispectral and SAR tasks through rendered inputs and compact LoRA adaptation, without training a new foundation model.

title: Network-Aware Forecasting on Wireless Access Points
abstract: Enterprise wireless access points (APs) are promising platforms for predictive machine learning (ML), but their primary responsibility remains providing wireless connectivity and network services. Predictive inference must therefore share an AP's CPU and memory with packet processing, Wi-Fi and IoT radio operations, and client management. This resource contention creates two risks: a model that performs well on proxy hardware may be too slow on the target AP, while a model that fits in isolation may still degrade network services under load. We define \textit{network-aware deployability} using two gates: qualification of the model and its execution path on the target AP, followed by validation of its execution profile under packet-service and forecasting constraints. Our benchmarks show that edge testbeds do not reliably capture target behavior. Across matched artifacts and serving settings, five model implementations run 6.1--19.1$\times$ slower on an AP than on a Raspberry Pi~5, while peak memory usage differs by up to 22\%. Moreover, two forecasting foundation models of similar size differ in AP latency by 19$\times$. When serving a smaller model across 13 parallel streams at a 30~s cadence under network saturation, default execution increases p99 round-trip time (RTT) by 76\% and reduces throughput by 7.06\%. Understanding these trade-offs is essential for live deployment if we aim to use APs for both networking and ML workloads.

title: Reward Hacking in the RL Loop: Oracle-Witnessed Localization and Repair of Reward-Model Exploits During Training
abstract: A replay-verified research artifact for measuring reward-channel exploitation during reinforcement learning. The frozen v1 study contains matched 300-step GRPO/LoRA arms on Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and GSM8K. The RLVR control has proxy-oracle gap 0; the deliberately gameable arm has 58/64 proxy successes versus 1/64 oracle successes (gap 0.890625). This is one-seed reward-hacking and amplification evidence, not a population estimate, frontier-model result, production-reward result, or capability-improvement claim. The archive includes exact manifests, hash-chained frame ledgers, final adapters, model-backed replay receipts, analysis, figures, paper, and executable controls.

title: Quantum Topology and Quantum Machine Learning Integration
abstract: Quantum topology, a fundamentally new field of mathematics, offers unique properties that can be leveraged to enhance machine learning algorithms. This paper explores the integration of quantum topology with machine learning, proposing a novel framework to achieve more powerful data analysis and model prediction. We outline the core claims, mechanism, and significance of this integration, emphasizing the potential for breakthroughs across diverse applications, particularly in areas demanding high-dimensional data and complex pattern recognition. The framework proposes a synergistic relationship between the inherent structural properties of quantum topology and the predictive capabilities of machine learning, ultimately aiming to push the boundaries of data-driven discovery.

title: Structured Quantum Stealth Computing Theory
abstract: Quantum Stealth Computing Theory explores the design of structured quantum computing systems, aiming to enhance security and efficiency through a novel approach to key distribution. This paper presents a theoretical framework centered around the manipulation of quantum entanglement to construct a 'structured' quantum computing paradigm. The core mechanism involves analyzing the inherent structure of the quantum computation to identify vulnerabilities and subsequently design a new, enhanced key distribution protocol. The resulting theory proposes a shift in how quantum keys are generated and distributed, offering a potential pathway toward more robust and scalable quantum technologies.

title: Adaptive Topology Learning for Neural Networks
abstract: This paper explores the concept of adaptive topology learning within neural networks, addressing the limitations of static topological neural networks. The core claim proposes that neural networks can actively learn their topology to adapt to evolving data and task requirements, ultimately leading to more efficient parallel computation. This is achieved through an internal topology learning module that dynamically adjusts network connections and node quantities based on performance metrics. The novelty lies in introducing this self-optimization capability, moving beyond the traditional static nature of topological neural networks. The paper details the theoretical framework, including the mathematical formulation of the topology learning process and the evaluation criteria. We present a methodology for continuous adaptation, emphasizing the role of feedback loops and optimization algorithms. The proposed approach aims to create neural networks that are not only powerful but also inherently adaptable and optimized for specific tasks. The key contributions include a novel framework for adaptive topology learning and a mathematical model to guide this process. ---

title: Module-Based Information Theory Assessment
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to information theory assessment utilizing a modular information theory (MINT) framework. The core claim is that MINT allows for dynamic adjustment of algorithm complexity based on input data characteristics, thereby improving algorithm efficiency. The framework decomposes the algorithm's complexity into distinct modules, which are adjusted automatically to optimally model the data's inherent complexity. This dynamic adaptation significantly enhances the ability of MINT to analyze complex data structures. We present a practical implementation demonstrating the framework's effectiveness in several benchmark datasets. The paper details the MINT framework's architecture, the complexity decomposition process, and its impact on performance across various data types. Finally, we discuss the limitations and potential future directions of this approach.

title: Self-Supervised Learning with Contrastive Predictive Coding and Temporal Regularization
abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) has achieved remarkable progress in recent years, particularly with contrastive predictive coding (CPC). However, CPC's performance often degrades when dealing with long-range dependencies within sequential data. This work addresses this limitation by augmenting CPC with a novel temporal regularization term. This regularization penalizes prediction errors not just based on the difference between the predicted and actual future states, but also based on the model's own predicted future states. This encourages temporal coherence and improves the model's ability to capture and utilize long-range dependencies. We demonstrate that this combined approach leads to significant improvements in learning performance compared to standard CPC, particularly in tasks requiring understanding of temporal sequences. The core claim of this work is that Contrastive predictive coding (CPC) can struggle with long-range dependencies in sequential data. The core mechanism is to augment CPC with a temporal regularization term that penalizes prediction errors based on the model's own predicted future states, enforcing temporal coherence. The novelty lies in the combination of CPC with this specific temporal regularization strategy. ---

title: Old Search Trees, New Fruits: A Comparative Analysis Review of AI Planning and Classical Search Revisited
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of AI Planning and Classical Search Revisited in the context of Artificial Intelligence. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of planning and search algorithms as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Artificial Intelligence.

title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence via Causal Inference Framework
abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) centered around causal inference. The core claim is to construct a system capable of not only explaining the decision-making process of AI models but also performing causal inference on those decisions. The proposed mechanism involves decomposing the model's decision process into a sequence of causal steps, utilizing causal graphs for modeling, and employing counterfactual reasoning for interpretation. Unlike existing XAI methods primarily focused on internal model explanations, this framework addresses the critical need for analyzing the causal relationships underlying AI decisions, offering a more robust and trustworthy approach to understanding and validating AI systems. The framework aims to provide insights into *why* a model made a specific decision, going beyond simply identifying which features contributed to the output. This work lays the groundwork for building AI systems that are not just accurate, but also transparent and accountable.

title: 自适应量子拓扑的量子信息存储与检索
abstract: Quantum information storage and retrieval represents a significant challenge in the field of quantum information science. Traditional approaches often rely on static quantum states, limiting the system's versatility. This paper explores the potential of utilizing self-adaptive quantum topology to design a novel quantum information storage and retrieval framework. We present a conceptual model demonstrating the dynamic adjustment of quantum states based on topological properties, offering a pathway towards more flexible and adaptable quantum data storage and retrieval. The core mechanism focuses on leveraging the inherent adaptability of quantum topology to enable instantaneous and robust quantum state manipulation. This research investigates the implications of this approach, emphasizing its potential to surpass the limitations of conventional methods.

title: Quantum State Dynamics Optimization
abstract: Quantum state dynamics optimization is a rapidly evolving field within quantum computing, aiming to enhance the performance of quantum algorithms through intelligent parameter adjustment. This paper presents a novel algorithm, Quantum State Dynamics Optimization (QSDO), that leverages the concept of dynamic topology to automatically optimize quantum state parameters. We introduce a method that iteratively adjusts the quantum state to minimize errors and maximize fidelity, addressing a key limitation of traditional parameter tuning methods. The core mechanism centers around constructing and manipulating a dynamic topology, allowing for continuous, adaptive parameter adjustments. The paper details the algorithm's implementation, demonstrates its effectiveness through simulations, and discusses its potential impact on quantum computation.

title: Graph-Based Quantum Computation Algorithm
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum computation algorithm based on graph theory, aiming to simplify quantum computations by leveraging graph structure characteristics. Traditional quantum computing often struggles with efficiently utilizing graph structures, leading to complex algorithms. Our approach transforms the core quantum computation process into a graph representation, employing graph nodes and edges to design an optimized quantum computation. The core mechanism focuses on reducing computational complexity through the intelligent design of the graph structure itself. This paper details the algorithm's architecture, the rationale behind the graph representation, and the resulting efficiency gains compared to traditional methods. We present preliminary results demonstrating the effectiveness of this algorithm in solving a specific benchmark problem, highlighting its potential for advancing quantum computing.

title: 基于多智能体协作的概率推理网络
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for probabilistic inference leveraging the power of multi-agent collaboration. The core idea is to distribute the inference task across a network of intelligent agents, each specializing in a particular subset of probabilistic information. Through a carefully designed collaboration mechanism, these agents collectively deduce and update global probability distributions. Furthermore, machine learning algorithms are employed to optimize the collaborative strategies, enhancing both the efficiency and accuracy of the inference process. Unlike traditional centralized approaches, this decentralized architecture offers scalability and robustness, particularly in scenarios involving large and complex datasets. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a theoretical analysis and outline key design considerations for implementing such a system. The primary contribution lies in the integration of multi-agent systems with probabilistic inference, leading to improved performance and adaptability.

title: Non-Symmetric Quantum Circuits: A Proof of Universal Computation and Architectural Design
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to quantum computation centered around non-symmetric quantum circuits. We provide a rigorous mathematical proof demonstrating the universal computational capabilities of these circuits under specific conditions. Furthermore, we propose a dedicated hardware architecture designed for efficient computation using non-symmetric quantum lines. This work challenges the traditional paradigm of symmetric quantum circuits and offers a new perspective on utilizing non-symmetric circuits for quantum computation. Our analysis leverages concepts such as quantum entanglement and decoherence, and highlights the potential for achieving enhanced computational performance through careful circuit design. The key contribution lies in establishing a framework for understanding and exploiting the unique properties of non-symmetric quantum circuits, paving the way for the development of more efficient and versatile quantum computing systems.

title: Solar Photovoltaic Generation Forecasting: A Review of Artificial Intelligence Approaches
abstract: The rapid global expansion of solar photovoltaic (PV) capacity has increased the operational need for accurate generation forecasting to support grid balancing, dispatch, and market participation. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods now dominate this research area, but the resulting literature is large and methodologically fragmented, making it difficult to establish which methods are used, what data they require, and where the principal gaps lie. This paper combines a bibliometric analysis of 3111 records retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection (2010–2026) with a technical synthesis of 27 highly cited studies published from 2022 onward, combining the most highly cited works with targeted additions from 2024–2025 covering specific methodological gaps. The bibliometric analysis shows exponential growth in annual output, from three publications in 2010 to 609 in 2025, with keyword evolution tracing a clear methodological trajectory from classical and fuzzy-logic approaches, through shallow and deep neural networks, to transformer- and attention-based architectures since 2023. The technical synthesis finds that classical machine learning remains competitive for day-ahead forecasting with well-structured numerical weather prediction inputs, that convolutional neural network–long short-term memory (CNN-LSTM) hybrids dominate the deep-learning literature, and that graph-based and transformer architectures address multi-site and multi-horizon forecasting, respectively. A comparison of reported results shows that absolute error metrics are not directly comparable across studies due to heterogeneous datasets, metrics, temporal resolutions, and climates, although relative improvements within controlled comparisons are directionally consistent. Seven research gaps are identified, including the absence of standardized benchmarks, limited public dataset availability, weak cross-region generalization, and underdeveloped uncertainty quantification.

title: Detect Then Rewrite: A Two-Stage Pipeline for Arabic Toxicity Moderation under Data Scarcity
abstract: Arabic harmful-content moderation is commonly framed as toxicity detection, but many practical settings also require safer alternatives to toxic text rather than only blocking or labeling it. We study Arabic toxicity handling as a low-resource detect–then–rewrite problem. The first stage classifies comments as normal, hate, or abusive using a multi-dialect Arabic encoder, while the second stage rewrites toxic inputs into neutral alternatives using an Arabic sequence-to-sequence model. title: Prospective Test of Audit Sufficiency and Allocation Identity in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: This preregistration specifies a prospective experiment testing whether standard retrieval audits are behaviorally sufficient to characterize finite context allocations in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The experiment constructs audit-equivalent context allocations that preserve the complete relevance-grade-by-position vector and therefore preserve precision@k, recall@k, nDCG@k, MRR@k, and MAP@k exactly, while varying the identities of metric-zero passages admitted to the finite context window. The primary outcome is the rate at which these identity-only reallocations change factual correctness. Secondary outcomes include canonical output change, identity-dose response, ordering sensitivity, and transport across datasets, retrievers, model families, and context capacities. This registration covers only the prospective RAG experiment. The broader manuscript also contains theoretical and previously conducted observational analyses that are not claimed to have been preregistered.

title: Prompt Before You Train: When Prompt Optimization Outperforms RLAIF for Small Language Models
abstract: Many social-good applications require small language models that can run locally and at low cost. When these models underperform, practitioners face a practical choice: invest in additional training using reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) or first try improving the prompt. We study this question in climate communication, where persuasive messaging is important for public engagement and environmental awareness. We compare RLAIF and iterative prompt optimization across four small language models (350M–1.5B parameters) and three persuasion principles: Authority, Social Proof, and Unity. Across most conditions, prompt optimization produced larger gains in externally judged rubric-adherence scores while requiring no additional model training. In contrast, RLAIF often improved its internal reward without producing corresponding improvements in externally evaluated performance. Further analysis revealed several forms of reward misalignment, including reward hacking and self-judge saturation. These model-based scores do not establish effects on human attitudes or behavior. The results support prompt optimization as a first step only within the evaluated climate-communication setting; subsequent training should be checked using evaluation outside its optimization loop. This approach can help resource-constrained organizations, including non-profits, educational institutions, community groups, and small public-sector agencies, test lower-cost interventions before model retraining.

title: SLIDEFORGE: An LLM Agent for Controllable Editing of Slides as Structured Artifacts
abstract: Current AI agents compellingly describe slides. However, AI-assisted slide editing requires more than understanding: the output must retain layout, style, component structure, and native editability. Towards, AI-assisted slide editing, existing agents operate on screenshots or weak document representations and often fragment coherent visual units, rasterize editable content, or break layout. In contrast, for controllable slide editing, we introduce an agentic framework, SLIDEFORGE, which builds a Deck State Graph, an executable slide state that links visual decomposition, native pptx object structure, and perceptual organization. By recovering human-referable components while retaining fine-grained editable structure, SLIDEFORGE supports theme-preserving reconstruction through slide-native operations and rendered-state verification. We further introduce an evaluation paradigm for controllable slide transformation that jointly measures component recovery, preservation, restyling consistency, visual quality, and native editability. Experiments show that SLIDEFORGE outperforms direct prompting, screenshot-based agents, and generic code-agent baselines across these dimensions. Code is available at https://github.com/UIUC-MONET/SLIDEFORGE.

title: Quantum Adaptive Distributed Optimization (QADO)
abstract: This paper introduces the Quantum Adaptive Distributed Optimization (QADO) framework, a novel approach to distributed optimization leveraging quantum entanglement for enhanced efficiency. Traditional distributed optimization methods often rely on static algorithms, limiting scalability and computational speed. QADO introduces a quantum-enhanced optimization process utilizing entanglement to achieve significantly reduced complexity and improved solution quality. We detail the framework's architecture, quantum entanglement implementation, and the resulting benefits observed through simulations and preliminary experiments. The paper concludes with a discussion of the potential impact of QADO on a wide range of optimization problems.

title: Dynamic Quantum State Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic quantum state optimization algorithm designed to enhance the performance of quantum computing, particularly in quantum simulation and parameter tuning. Traditional quantum algorithms often rely on fixed parameters, necessitating a more adaptable approach. Our proposed algorithm leverages the dynamic evolution of quantum states to optimize quantum states, achieving superior results in these critical areas. This research addresses the limitations of existing methods by offering a robust and efficient solution for parameter adjustment and optimization within quantum systems. The core mechanism centers on continuously adjusting quantum states to maximize performance metrics, offering a significant advancement in quantum computation.
